This establishes its name. Furthermore, through the teaching, the wisdom arising from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) is produced; through reasoning, the wisdom arising from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) is produced;
and through practice, the wisdom arising from cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) is produced. By means of these three types, one attains the fruit. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"It is not logical for the latencies of hearing and so forth to produce no fruit. Moreover, there are three categories of naming established in the sūtras: first, based on person and dharma; second, based on analogy; or...

Whether single or paired, they alternate without fixed order. Why is this so? Regarding the reliance on persons: it is to cause [beings] to know how to cultivate the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ānulomikāḥ saṃrañjanīyā dharmāḥ*).

As for the six points of harmonious respect, these refer to harmony in the three types of action (*trividha-karma*), harmony in precepts and views, and harmony in giving and material benefits. Regarding the reliance on the Dharma:

it is to cause [beings] to know the definitive meaning through the principles of the definitive teachings, including the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna doctrines. Regarding the reliance on analogies: it is for the purpose of leading [beings].
Because sentient beings are dull-witted, it is necessary to manifest both the Dharma and its analogies; for through extensive analogies, the meaning is clarified.

Furthermore, whether from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*) or their locations, all are subsumed within the category of "Dharma," as the name "Dharma" is broad in scope. Following this principle, the establishment of names for the teachings can be inferred from whatever is cited;

fearing prolixity, I shall not cite them all here. In discussing the general establishment of names, nothing surpasses this. One who observes what has been inherited and received will have no doubts regarding this truth. Truly.
In the *Treatise on the Three Pitakas* (*Dì sānzàng lùn*), the author himself provides an explanation of the titles.

The commentary states that regarding the categories of "based on the person" and "based on the Dharma," those named after specific events are followed by those first named after persons, such as the *Śrīmālā*, the *Amitābha*, and the *Vimalakīrti*.
These are all named after persons. Those named after the Dharma include, for example, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Those named according to both the sense of being based on a person and based on the Dharma include, for example, the *Vimalakīrti*.
Those named after metaphors and based on the Dharma include this sutra and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*. Those named after their location are, namely...

The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra was preached on the summit of Mount Gayā. Not only are the titles of various sūtras established based on their dharma-meanings, but this very [sūtra] is a "Dharma Chapter" (dharmapada).
Furthermore, its chapters may be fully understood by considering them according to the person, the dharma, and the metaphor.

The Commentary states: "Peace and happiness exist in the cause; 'manifest' refers to the present life. 'Within the name of a single meaning' clarifies that this peace and happiness does not extend to both cause and fruit.

As for 'the name of a single meaning,' it means that the person who is able to receive and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* attains freedom from calamity and fear in their current body, experiences joy in body and mind, and receives the respect of others and offerings—this is the peace and happiness of the present life."

This is taken from the perspective of meaning. Alternatively, it may be that "peace and happiness" (an-le) resides within the causal practice for the sake of the fruit; thus, it is described according to these two meanings.

In this case, receiving and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in the present life is the cause, while receiving the retribution of peace and happiness in a future life is the fruit. "Seeing" (*jian*) refers to the present manifestation.
The term "Middle" (Chung) also carries this meaning. When the jeweled stupa emerged within the assembly on Vulture Peak, it was subsumed under a single meaning;

since it did not clarify the "one who sees," it does not constitute two meanings. If "seeing" refers to the act of seeing, then it constitutes two meanings because the term "Middle" encompasses both the capacity [to see] and the object.
Here, the "seer" is the person who sees, and the "stupa" is the stupa that is seen—the object seen. Since both the subject and the object are titled together, it constitutes two meanings.
...included. Therefore, it is said that [the classification] is indeterminate (the same applies to the "Dharma Master" chapter).
Third, there was Upper Dinglin Temple; there was also Lower Dinglin Temple, just as Mount Song at the Eastern Capital has both East Xianju Temple and West Xianju Temple.
As for Waguan Temple, it was originally the tile-roofed official residence (wa-fang) which was donated to become a temple. Thus...
This was done for the sake of its name. As for the kingdom of Khotan (*Yutian*), it is the "Land of the Breast.
Before a shrine of that country’s deity, a young boy emerged from the earth, and in that very spot, a breast likewise emerged from the ground.
When this small boy was hungry, he would go there to eat. After he had grown up, one person took charge of him and established him as the ruler of that country.
Prince, it is therefore called the Land of the Breast (Nanyue).

The Commentary states: "Regarding the five errors and three difficulties: first, the error of inversion (*pratyāpatti*). The Sanskrit original is frequently inverted; [the translation] corrects these into the proper order.
For example, in Sanskrit it is said *evam mayā śrutam* (Thus have I heard), while here it is rendered as *如是我聞* (Thus have I heard). In Sanskrit it is *pāramitā*.
One should say "reaching the other shore," yet here it is said "reaching the other shore" [in reverse]. *Vajra* in Sanskrit means "able to cut," yet here it is said "Able-to-cut Vajra" and so forth;

all such instances are inversions of this kind. In the West, one calls for "rice" because one eats only when there is rice; here, however, it is called "eating rice," which is precisely an inversion of the correct order.

Second is the loss of the distinction between substance (*vyañjana*) and expression (*nāman*): the Sanskrit term is predominantly substantial (*dravya*), whereas here it is predominantly expressive (*nāman*).
Regarding the phrasing: as it says in the Sanskrit original, "The fourfold assembly sat in a dense cluster, gazing directly at the World-Honored One with unblinking eyes.
That [Sanskrit] expression is the substance; here [in Chinese], it is said, "Gazing up at the World-Honored One, his eyes never for a moment leaving him," which is the literal wording.

Furthermore, it says, "May the Heavenly Lord bring peace and rain, and may the grains ripen in peace. It also says, "Bamboo shoots, bamboo, and reeds; the lion’s majestic stride, the Buddha. And this...
At the time of translating the sutra, it was said: "The heavens see humans, and humans see the heavens.

Master Rui remarked that it should rather say, "Humans and devas intersect, so that both may see one another," and this principle is not found in this single passage alone. For instance, when the Buddha preached the Dharma, what text could fail to convey his intent?

His purpose lay in benefiting others; yet their faculties differ—some sharp, some dull—and their natures diverge—some foolish, some wise. If he were to speak with such literal directness, the foolish...
Wisdom is opened up simultaneously. If one were to explain it through literary elaboration, wisdom would fail to penetrate the obscurity.

Therefore, we take only the meaning and not the literary form. Direct language reveals the meaning, whereas flowery rhetoric obscures the principle. Now, by employing literary exposition, we lose the original text of the Sūtra; even if one were to uphold it, they would lack the power [to understand it].
Thus, we set aside this fault. Third, regarding expansion and abbreviation: the Sanskrit version is mostly expansive, while this translation is mostly abbreviated. For example, *buddha*.
*Dharma* here refers to the Buddha-dharma. There were four ways in which [the translators] deviated by adopting or rejecting [the text] according to their own inclinations.

Regarding the extensive explanations of various preferences, all of which were inconvenient for both mind and speech, they concealed those textual passages. Thus, it became as if there were five distinct natures;

they clearly translated out the texts concerning the five natures while concealing the meaning of the single nature (*ekayāna*). Those who take the single nature as their school clearly revealed the meaning of the [single] nature.

This text obscures the meaning of the five natures and conceals one's own sentiments, involving both acceptance and rejection. Fifth, the deletion of what precedes and the abbreviation of what follows is an error.

When the World-Honored One preached the Dharma, he frequently repeated what was stated earlier when speaking of what followed; yet in this current translation, only the latter remains while the preceding repetitive text has been deleted.
Therefore, this is established as an error. It is also said that the preceding is concluded by way of association; that is to say, all the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata...
These instances of using parables to illustrate the meaning are all omitted here. For example, in the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta," there is praise for the sutra;

in the "Devadatta-parivarta," there is incidental discussion of past events concerning the upholding of the sutra; it is only upon reaching the "Dhāraṇī-parivarta" that one is first exhorted to uphold the sutra. The "Pūrva-yoga-parivarta" follows this same pattern:
wishing to speak of the "illusory city," it first clarifies the past events of the sixteen princes under the Greatly Penetrating and Victorious Wisdom (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū).
This refers to the matter [of the treatise]. Only afterward does he provide a simile, which is called a "collateral conclusion" (*pārśvabandha*).

Regarding the three things that are not easily [understood]: first, the difference between eras is not easily [resolved]. The Buddha was born during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty and passed away during the time of King Mu of the Zhou.

Since antiquity and the present differ, the methods of preaching the Dharma are also distinct. This [work] is now translated anew, differing from ancient texts. To equate the ancient with the present is, in principle, not...

Indeed, the matter admits of no other possibility. The gap between the ignorant and the wise is vast and not easily bridged. Formerly, when the Dharma was compiled, all were equally called "worthy sages" (*ārya*);

the two emptinesses and the principle of wisdom were fused as one. Now, upon re-examining the records, people are found to be collectively confined to the rank of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Since the distinction between the ignorant and the wise has thus emerged, [the situation is clear].
Therefore, it is not an easy matter. Thirdly, there is the difficulty of trepidation and arrogance.

In the past, when the Dharma-treasury was being compiled, people were as cautious and fearful as this, for they feared that losing even a single word would render the sutra powerless. Now, those who perform translations are as casual and indifferent as this.

They do not give rise to reverence; they omit the preceding and abbreviate the subsequent, hence it is said that "it is not easy. It is also said that "there is a distinction between ordinary beings and sages, thus it is not easy.

Now one is an ordinary being and formerly was a sage; therefore, it is not easy. Furthermore, the term "jing-jing" (cautious/anxious) describes the appearance of one treading on ice, fearing that by stepping upon the ice, one might sink and die.
This refers to the Arhat’s state of *jing-jing*: fearing he might lose the holy words and fall into the realm of ordinary beings.
This is because [the Buddha] enters into birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of one volume in seven fascicles (one hundred and twenty-five sheets). Other meanings are as explained in the first draft.

Regarding the reason why that ancient master placed the "Entrusting" chapter (*parīndanā-parivarta*) at the beginning, there are four reasons. First, because of the admonition regarding the punishment of Gadgadasvara.
The commentary (*shu*) states: "In the 'Entrusting' chapter (*zhulèi pǐn*), it is commanded that the manifested Buddhas each return to their own lands.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound arrives, why is he cautioned against conceiving thoughts of inferiority regarding this land? Second, because he alone pays homage to Prabhūtaratna;
the commentary states that the passage following the emergence from below the earth and the prostration to the manifested Buddhas is where this occurs. Third, the contemplation..."

Regarding "because Avalokiteśvara offers the jewel," the commentary states: "Avalokiteśvara’s offering of the jewel should not be understood as merely two portions"; the following text constitutes this point.

Regarding "because Bhaiṣajyarāja receives the command," it says: "Furthermore, since the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment) clarifies the entrustment," the following text constitutes this point.
As for the "two matters being contradictory," this refers to the fact that while the emanation bodies and Prabhūtaratna reside at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, Śākyamuni [is elsewhere].

[The text] commands each to return to their own lands; how then could it be that the emanation-body of Prabhūtaratna goes one way while remaining another? (Therefore, it is said that these two matters are contradictory).

Regarding the seventh difficulty concerning the distinction between the pure and the defiled: [the text] states that when Mañjuśrī’s ocean-like assembly was about to arrive here and was already present at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, flowers suddenly appeared.
This citation is erroneous; it should refer to the time when the ocean-like assembly from the Dragon Palace was about to arrive, [and the flowers appeared] within Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Originally there were no flowers appearing; it was simply that Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva sat upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower.
As for the assembly in the Dragon Palace sitting on lotus flowers, they appeared simultaneously with the [Bodhisattva’s] flower; it was not a prior manifestation. This too is untenable.
Since it is said that [Mañjuśrī] arrived, how could flowers suddenly appear? If it were as Gadgadasvara says—that flowers appear when one arrives—then it would be understandable.

The Commentary states: "Since it is not that joy arises from hearing the Jewel of the Dharma—meaning it is not that joy arises from hearing the words of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) throughout the three turnings of the wheel—it must be that joy arises from seeing the Guest Buddha depart. This is also incorrect;
for one may indeed experience joy simply upon hearing the conclusion of the three turnings.

The Commentary states: "It is simply because he first exercised his supernatural power that he manifested the Pure Land. This subsequent passage reconciles the previous external objection regarding the transformation of the physical form by the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara.

Thus, we know that the entrustment (*parindanā*) should logically occur earlier. Therefore, this section should read: "When the World-Honored One was about to open the precious stūpa, he immediately gathered his body;

first, by means of his supernormal transformations, he caused the defilements to become pure. Since this land has already been purified, how could it be [otherwise] for the *Śuddhāvasa* (Pure Abode) of the *Puṣpābhijña* (Flower-Knowledge)?
King Jñāna Buddha earnestly admonished Gadgadasvara: "Go to that land, but do not conceive thoughts of inferiority.

Gadgadasvara then replied: "Although I, Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva, possess superior virtue, my cognitive obscurations have not yet been extinguished; the mind of grasping and rejecting still remains within me.
Because that land is pure while this land is fundamentally defiled, I fear that Gadgadasvara might perceive both lands as pure."
They perceive the characteristics of this defiled land and give rise to criticism and disparagement; therefore, that Buddha admonishes them.
This is just as a ruler of the barbarian tribes might say, "It is not as good as the decline of the Central States," seeing both sides without error.

It is not meant that the Buddha of Wondrous Sound has come here, nor that the Buddhas who have manifested their bodies have already returned, such that one could say this land is solely defiled and not pure. Since one looks up from below, this interpretation is also logically consistent (and so forth).
The Commentary states: "Just as although one is in a pure land, one still sees Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa," and so forth, up to "the transformation is not seen only from above by those below.
This refers to the Master of the Commentary [Jizang], who provides an analogy that within a pure land there are also impure lands.

This means that the various emanation Buddhas each command their attendants to take handfuls of flowers and proceed to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Heavenly Lifespan," Mañjuśrī emerges from the ocean. All together...

Regarding the visit to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa: since it occurs within the "Chapter on the Heavenly Longevity" (Tianshou pin) prior to the "Chapter on Entrustment" (Zhulei pin), and as the emanated bodies still remain and all these lands are pure, how could there be a Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa?
How does this preclude that within a pure land there may also be an impure land, because one sees the lower from the higher, and because it can be designated by the name of its original location?
Therefore, the statement that they "proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa" is logically unassailable. Furthermore, within the "Chapter on the Stūpas" (Tapin)...

There is a Pure Land; it does not preclude the existence of that Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains admonitions and punishments, why should it not also contain the Pure Land?

Thus we know that the stūpa is also Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and its inclusion within the Pure Land is not contradictory. Although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains admonitions, it is nonetheless subsumed under the Pure Land.
Therefore, we know that the entrustment (*parindanā*) ought to come at the end.
The Commentary states: "The passage beginning with 'The two Buddhas were together' and following clarifies the previous specific objection.

This is because Miaoyin (Gandhahastin) pays homage and Avalokiteśvara offers the pearl. If one were to say that only the two Honored Ones remain in the assembly while the emanations have returned—referring to the *Tianshou pin* (Chapter on the Lifespan), where Mañjuśrī pays homage only to the feet of the two Honored Ones and does not pay homage to the emanations."
It is also called "The Two Honored Ones Return to Their Assembly after Manifesting Their Emanations. Thus, one knows that the intent of the dedication is distinct.

How can this be used as a precedent to require universal dedication? Furthermore, some speak of the power of the Dharma-protection, claiming that the "Universal Worthy Chapter" and the subsequent chapter showing [the Buddha] are the "Measuring Heaven and Earth Chapter," not the "Entrustment.
This lacks scriptural authority; being a spurious sutra, it cannot be taken as a basis.
[The commentary] explains (and so forth).
Regarding the placement of the "Chapter on the Entrustment" (Zhūlèi pǐn)—whether it precedes or follows [the main body of the sūtra]—there is a specific reason for each.

As for the fact that the "Chapter on the Entrustment" does not appear at the end of the sūtra, there are various interpretations by different schools (*zhūjiā*) based on a single principle. If one says that the entrustment should also be [included here], it is likewise appropriate.
Regarding the fact that [the Buddha] was in front and not behind: when Gadgadasvara requested an audience with Prabhūtaratna, the gate of the stupa had already opened.
At that time, Śākyamuni was already there with Prabhūtaratna; thus, Gadgadasvara subsequently beheld the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna.
Furthermore, this Buddha made a vow, desiring to open his own stupa, and consequently gathered his emanations. Since he has already returned, it cannot be that Śākyamuni opens it.
Since Gadgadasvara saw the Stupa of Prabhūtaratna, there was the error of opening it again; thus we know that those who open it now are simply identical to the assembly of the previous chapter.

In the text concerning Prabhūtaratna, the manifestation of the divided bodies is included therein. Inferring from this, the instruction given to Gadgadasvara on the following day was originally intended for an impure setting;
therefore, the entrustment (parīndanā) ought to have been placed at the beginning. Furthermore, if one were to say that the entrustment should be placed at the end—
As for its not being placed at the beginning: at the end of the "Universal Worthy Chapter" (Samantabhadra-parivarta), the great assembly has already departed after joyfully prostrating themselves.

Thus we know there are no further chapters. Furthermore, if one were to say that the entrustment (*parindanā*) of all sutras must occur at the very end of the scripture and should not be placed at the beginning, what contradiction would there be in principle for an entrustment to occur midway? For instance, the titles of various sutras are all established at the end of the scriptures.

In the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the question regarding the name of the scripture is asked immediately, and the Buddha responds by stating, "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*," and so forth.
Why is it that the teaching of the sutra is interrupted before completion to ask this question? It is because the intention is to ensure its immediate practice and observance.

As for why this chapter on Entrustment (*Parīndanā*) is spoken here, prior to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*, it is because the teaching of the One Vehicle (*Ekayāna*) throughout the three turnings of the wheel of Dharma has been concluded, and [the teaching] is now being handed over.

The entrustment is circulated. In the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* and other sections, the causes and conditions for the weightiness of this sutra are explained extensively, so that those who receive and uphold it may give rise to reverence and respect;
this is likewise unobjectionable. Both the preceding and the following [sections] are thus valid (and so forth).
Furthermore, regarding the clarification of the sequence of chapters and the matters concerning my prior and subsequent [teachings]:

as for why the "Chapter on the Wondrous Sound" (*Ghoṣadatta-parivarta*) follows the "Chapter on the Medicine King" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*), if we follow the scriptural text, at the single assembly on Vulture Peak, the Bodhisattva Ghoṣadatta had not yet arrived at Vulture Peak when the "Chapter on the Medicine King" was being preached.
It was only after the threefold exposition of the Dharma that Ghoṣadatta arrived. How is this known? By the mention of Ghoṣadatta.
[The Buddha] said, "The Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara has come for the sake of hearing the Lotus Sutra.
Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) also said, "In the land of the Buddha Ratnatejobhyudgatarāja, I heard from afar that this Sahā world was preaching the Lotus Sutra;
I have come here from there. Since he stated, "I have come to this place for the sake of hearing this sutra," it is known that [this occurred] within the three assemblies.
When Gadgadasvara arrives—if he had not previously come to this assembly—then according to the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta*, it says:
"Let him come; let him hear the Dharma. What Dharma is he to hear? Within this chapter, there is no mention of him preaching the sutra. Furthermore, at the end of this chapter, it says:

"Gadgadasvara arrives here," yet within the same chapter, it immediately states that he returns to his own country. If he has already returned to his country, then regarding the subsequent chapters on Avalokiteśvara and others... [text fragment ends]
One could not even hear the sound. Why, then, did you say that you had come here for the sake of hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?

Thus we know that Gadgadasvara had already arrived here during the three assemblies. As for the statement that he now wishes to see Prabhūtaratna but cannot see him, it is because during those three assemblies the gate of the stupa had not yet been opened and the ground was still defiled. Judging by this, it follows that one can only see the Buddha after this point.

This is because the gate of the stupa opened due to the gathering of the emanated bodies; thus, it is said that they "saw" [the Buddha]. Based on this principle, these two meanings stand side by side and are not mutually related.

Furthermore, it is asked: If that is so, why is it listed after the "Chapter on the Dharani of the Medicine King" (Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta) in the "Chapter on the Wondrous Sound" (Gandavyūha-parivarta)?
Therefore, why is this chapter placed first among the three cycles? The explanation is as follows:

Although the arrival of Gadgadasvara is for the purpose of hearing the sutra and thus precedes [the other events], it is not appropriate to explain it first within the textual exposition of the meaning.

For words should not be repeated, and meanings should not be discussed in tandem. Since the assembly of Gadgadasvara belongs to the events of the Vulture Peak gathering, at the time the sutra was compiled, Ānanda...

It is difficult to recite [in a single breath]. Generally, when narrating events, they are arranged in chronological order. Within a single assembly, there may be an extremely large number of matters and dharmas;
although the *Miaoyin* (Wondrous Sound) [chapter] occurs earlier in the assembly, this category has been arranged to reside later.
If it were not so, how could it come within one chapter and then depart within another? Therefore, we know that a "chapter" (*pin*) refers to a category (*lei*) with respect to the subject matter.

Because they are identical, they are arranged into chapters. Furthermore, it is asked: Since the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* assembly [of the *Lotus Sūtra*] consists of three cycles, it should correspond to the preceding treatise;

yet, as this is now explained later, by what principle or logic is it to be understood? It is like people in the world: regarding the relative status of uncles and nephews, the nephew is inferior while the uncle is superior—this is universally known.
However, there may be cases where a nephew is older and an uncle is younger; if such were established as the norm, it would not be so.
Because a nephew is older in age, he is included among the category of uncles; it is not because an uncle is inferior in age that his nephew later becomes devoid of conduct.

Now, regarding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other chapters, the ritual protocol is as follows. If one follows this principle, what fault could there be in the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara being thus admonished?
Furthermore, in the "Avalokiteśvara Chapter," there is the phrase: "The Honored One who possesses the perfect and wondrous marks. This was originally placed there by the compilers;
it should have been formulated as prose (gadya), but because the text was too short, they did not compose separate prose sections for it.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also contains this same principle. As for Queen Śrīmālā, she was the daughter of King Prasenajit, born of Queen Mallikā.
She was married as a consort to the King of Ayodhyā, who resided more than a thousand *li* away. In that kingdom, the Buddha-dharma had previously not existed.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma at the Jetavana Monastery, the parents, knowing their daughter’s intelligence, sent a letter to summon her, describing the inconceivable virtue and wisdom of the Buddha. Upon receiving her mother’s letter, Queen Vaśiṣṭhā immediately spoke:
The verse says: "Now I hear the voice of the Buddha, such as has never before existed in the world. If it be true, then I shall offer worship. He further spoke in verse:
"I look up with reverence to the World-Honored Buddha, who has appeared for the sake of the world; you should likewise harbor compassion for me."
"May you surely grant that I may behold you. Having spoken this verse, the Buddha manifested his subtle and wondrous body in the sky.

The compilers of the canon then composed a verse, saying: "At the very moment this thought arose, the Buddha appeared in the sky, universally radiating pure light and manifesting his incomparable form.
Queen Śrīmālā and her retinue bowed their heads at his feet in prostration. According to this verse:
This is prose; as for its being rendered into verse by way of convenience, it is similar to the passage in this sutra beginning with "The Honored One Complete with Sublime Marks.
These are the words of Śrīmālā. The verse says: "Out of compassion, protect me; cause the seeds of the Dharma to grow.
In this life and in future births, may the Buddha always sustain me."
"The curses and various poisons shall return to the person who cast them. An external objection asks: "Does this not mean that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would instead harm living beings?
The explanation says: Suppose there is a person who harbors a grudge against another; they employ talismans and incantations, using various poisons [to curse their enemy].

Desiring to kill another person, that person was subsequently subjected to a curse. Becoming aware that their own body and mind were uneasy, they immediately returned to single-mindedly and with a sincere heart reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara.
Because the roots of goodness from reciting Avalokiteśvara increased, all poisons were completely eliminated.
Although that person continued to curse the other, because their evil mind had accumulated much malice and they did not recite the name of Avalokiteśvara, focusing instead solely on killing—

This is harmful; therefore, it violates [the principle of] non-harming. This is the lingering calamity of accumulated evil. When misfortune and wickedness have accumulated, how could one be a bodhisattva?
Furthermore, although he was struck, it did not cause his death; rather, it was intended to cause him to give rise to a wholesome mind.

As in the aforementioned passage from this sutra, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging was reviled with foul language by the fourfold assembly; because of that angry abuse, he caused the fourfold assembly—
For a thousand kalpas they fall into hell; although they initially encounter suffering, because they later give rise to the bodhicitta, this case is likewise so—what doubt can there be?
Now, regarding the Bodhisattva’s salvation from suffering through various skillful means: if there is initial suffering followed by happiness, the Bodhisattva will save them.
This refers to cases such as those who were constantly disparaged (*Sadāparibhūta*) or those subjected to curses and the like. If, however, there is initial happiness...

Regarding those who experience happiness later: the Bodhisattva rescues them as well. Regarding those who experience suffering first and suffering later, the Bodhisattva does not rescue them. Regarding those who experience happiness first and suffering later, the Bodhisattva likewise does not rescue them (and so forth).
The Commentary states: "It is like a skilled hunter who is adept at capturing bears and *bharunda* (grizzly bears). Suppose there is a bear in a deep cave;
the hunter wishes to capture it and, using a three-pronged iron fork, holds the head forward while gripping the handle from behind.

He first strikes it with a stone, whereupon the bear’s rage is provoked and it rushes directly toward the man, unaware that the iron fork has already pierced its chest. Once it has rushed [forward]...

It cannot be avoided; it will persist until death. To explain this according to the intended meaning of the parable: the initial desire to harm another person corresponds to a wicked man’s incantations and the administration of poison.
Later, when one approaches being impaled by an iron fork, this corresponds to the matter of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva returning the [retribution] to the original person.

Here, the iron fork is used as a metaphor for Avalokiteśvara, and the bear and the *bhi* (a type of large carnivorous beast) are used as metaphors for those who administered the poison (and so forth).
Furthermore, it is like a skilled physician who expertly employs counteractive medicines. There was a man suffering from dropsy, his body as large as a jar.
His brothers could think of no remedy; they heard that *bhallātaka* seeds are incompatible with alcohol, so they thought he should be given them to eat.
Later, they had him drink wine, which ultimately meant he would not live—he was left with nothing but death. After the patient had taken the *bhallātaka* seeds, he became extremely ill.
He was parched with thirst, so they gave him two *liang* of wine, which he drank all at once. After a short while, they looked at him and saw that he was on the verge of death;
only a trace of life remained. After looking at him for a little longer, they saw water flowing in torrents from beneath the ground.
When they examined his body, it was as before, without any change. His brothers asked, "How does your body feel? He replied, "Today, there must surely be a way to live."
Furthermore, one might consume five sheng of gruel all at once; thus we know that a medicine taken in reverse is precisely such a case.
Although it may cause harm initially, it will certainly be beneficial later. The Bodhisattva’s saving of sentient beings is also like this.

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (commentary), "Since the verse does not contradict the fundamental tenet," this wording is erroneous. It should instead read: "Although there is harm, it does not contradict the fundamental tenet.

Those who read the *Śāstra* appear to be deliberating upon this verse. The intended meaning of these words is to explain the passage concerning how the curses and various poisons [directed at others] return to the person themselves;
that is to say, although there may be harm initially, there will necessarily be benefit later on.

The Commentary states: Regarding that explanation which uses the sunlight as a metaphor for the identity of the vehicles (*yāna*), it clarifies that in the "Parable of the Poor Son," the former poor son is shown to be identical to the elder.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says, "The vehicle is one. Now, the metaphor of the clouds and rain is taught to show that those who ride upon it are all equal.
Although the single rain is the same, the principles received by each are distinct; although the sunlight is one, the clarity received differs. That [text] adds the dharma...
The intent of the *Huā jīng* (Flower Sūtra) is thus. The commentators of the present day do not permit the existence of any further "sunlight" metaphors.

Furthermore, neither the *Zhèngfǎ huā jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), nor the *Miaofǎ liánhuā jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), nor their commentaries contain the metaphor of sunlight. Within the commentaries, regarding the explanation of the seven metaphors and the three equalities, there is likewise no mention of sunlight.
As for the "four following and three reversing": the four refers to the *Zhèngfǎ*, *Miàofǎ*, and *Běn* [sūtras].

The treatise supplements the *Sūtra on the Added Dharma* (Tiānfǎ jīng), as it ranks fourth. Regarding the "three contradictions": these three original sūtras and treatises contradict the preceding passage from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* which uses the absence of sunlight as a metaphor;
hence they are called the "three contradictions. Furthermore, they contradict the general tenor of the Great Vehicle's universal principle.
To say they are non-existent does not contradict established principles. According to Master Zàn, he did not permit the commentator [Jizang] to refute the passage concerning the "sunlight.
How is this known? For even in the *Lotus Sūtra* there is a passage regarding the identity of vehicles; one should say that three follow two, rather than being contrary to them.
Since both are equally the universal path and the sacred teaching, why must one be refuted? If it is argued that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed a commentary on the *Lotus Sūtra*:

Regarding the seven similes and the three vehicles explained [in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*], if one claims they do not exist simply because there is no textual passage mentioning "sunlight," then consider the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This too was commented upon by Vasubandhu; according to the sūtra, it should properly contain eight types of characteristics.

Why does the treatise explain only four—namely, the characteristic of a person (*pudgala*), the characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva*), the characteristic of a life-span (*jīva*), and the characteristic of a self (*ātman*)—without explaining the remaining four? How could that sūtra... [be otherwise]?
Since this passage is absent from the middle [of the text], we know that it cannot necessarily be taken as proof based on the treatise (and so forth).
Furthermore, regarding this single chapter on Avalokiteśvara that has circulated separately: since the Dharma first flowed eastward, over nine hundred years have passed.
Of the sūtras and śāstras translated during this time, there are seven types in total: first, single-text editions; second, double-text translations; and third, incomplete editions.

Regarding the scriptures: 1. Single-text scriptures; 2. Doubtful scriptures; 3. Excerpted scriptures; 4. Apocryphal scriptures; 5. Scriptures corresponding to auspicious omens. As for what are called "single-text scriptures," these are such works as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others, because they were not translated more than once.
Since their first translation, it has been heard that only the scholar Xie Lingyun of the southern region re-collated and corrected their phrasing, but no separate translations were made.
Second, regarding "re-translated" (or double-translated) scriptures, such as the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, and others have all been translated multiple times. Third, regarding those that are "missing" (*kue-pen*):

although their titles appear in the catalogs, neither the Sanskrit originals nor any previous translations exist that have circulated in the world. Fourth, regarding those that are "doubtful" (*yi*): such as the *Dharmapada-sūtra*.
These works accord with the principles of the Mahāyāna; however, they lack Sanskrit originals, and there is no record of their period of translation or the translators.
They were extracted from [other texts], such as the Avalokiteśvara Chapter and others, or from the *Bahuśruta-prajñāpāramitā* (Many-Hearted Prajñā), like the *Ullambana Sūtra*.
These lack the opening formula "Thus have I heard" and lack the concluding statement "Rejoicing, they practiced accordingly."
All of these are examples of this. Regarding the six types of forgeries: such as the *Tiangong jing* (Scripture of the Heavenly Lord), which involves incantations to bewitch Yi Zhu and Zhi Gong, etc.
As the *Tiangong jing* says: "Pure and clear, empty and void; holding a golden pitcher in hand, pushing out the voice to summon the masters, he enters straight into the lecture hall."
It is further said that Mañjuśrī served as the *dujiang* (Chief Lecturer) and Samantabhadra served as the *weina* (Rector), and so forth;
these are all human compositions and are not the Buddha’s teaching. As for the *Qiyingshui jing*, it is the *Gao Wang Guanshiyin Jing*. Emperor Gao Huan had a person die.
Because he focused his mindfulness on Avalokiteśvara, he received [the scripture] in a dream. Later, when he went to the marketplace, he passed through three sword-strokes without dying.
One should know that all these circumstances stem from the name bestowed by Gao Huan; therefore, it is called the *Gāowáng Guānshìyīn Jīng* (The Scripture of Avalokiteśvara of King Gao).
Fifth, the sequence of the chapters is elucidated. According to ancient tradition, it is said: "The Sūtra Piṭaka is sought through its sequential order;
the Vinaya Piṭaka is sought through its causal origins; the Abhidharma Piṭaka is sought through the investigation of essential nature and characteristics.

Regarding the investigation of essential nature and characteristics, this solely clarifies the dharmas that are with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, mundane or supramundane; as for their essential natures, there is no further sequential order.
Because it is able to generate wisdom. Regarding those who seek the *Vinaya-piṭaka* through its causes and conditions:

within the Vinaya, it clarifies only by whom a transgression was committed and how this precept came to exist; it clarifies many causes and conditions such as "this precept exists because a certain person committed an offense.

These are all matters of fact (*vastu-dharma*), possessing neither the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) nor a fixed sequential order; they are subsumed solely under the *Vinaya-piṭaka*. In contrast, the *Sūtra-piṭaka* possesses a sequential order.

Regarding "seeking": this refers to the teachings of the sūtras, wherein the names and meanings of preceding and succeeding sections are linked like hooks and chains, primarily clarifying the sequence of the chapters—the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination.
This is subsumed solely within the Sūtra Piṭaka.
The Commentary states: "To guide them back to the path by means of the One Reality" is because they have regressed from the bodhicitta.

Having previously heard the teachings of the Mahāyāna, they later neglected and forgot them, regressing to seek the Hīnayāna. Now, one desires to cause them to return to their original source; therefore, this is what is being introduced.
Therefore, it is said that this guides them back upon their path home. Thus, the second chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"In the past, I taught you to aspire to the Buddha-way, yet you have now completely forgotten it, claiming instead that you have already attained extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
I now wish to cause you to remember your original vow and the path you were to practice. To "return to one's traces" means to return to the traces of what was practiced in former times.
"Wisdom that raises up skillful means and responds appropriately to those of superior faculties": "wisdom that raises up" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*), while "skillful means" refers to *upāya*.
Thus, the "Chapter on Skillful Means" states: "The wisdom of the Buddhas is extremely profound and immeasurable.

Regarding the phrase "the words expound divine power and ferry one across to the abstruse principles," this refers to the fact that the gate of their wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter (it should be noted that the quoted passage here is cited in reverse order).
In the *Śāstra* (Commentary), the explanation of the "Parable Chapter" states: "The text for the summary and the bestowal of the prediction is brief...
as far as 'entrusting it to that summary and bestowing the prediction upon him,' etc. Master Zàn said: "This statement is erroneous.

If one were to claim that because the text for the summary is brief, it does not constitute a separate chapter and is instead explained by being attached to the 'Parable Chapter,' then why does [the text] further state 'entrusting'?"
The preceding text is extremely brief; I shall briefly clarify this following the "Chapter on Supernatural Powers" (Ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra-parivarta). How could it be that a separate chapter is produced?

Thus, we know that the commentators were exceedingly reckless. As for contemporary interpreters who claim that the chapters—such as those where Śāriputra summarizes and recounts, or where the Tathāgata bestows predictions—are all merely analogies, they are indeed similes (*aupamya*).
What prevents them all from being given the same name, the "Simile Chapter" (*Aupamya-parivarta*)?
Is it not redundant to say that [the previous argument] was profoundly mistaken? Now, I further challenge the Dharma Master of Bingzhou:

if you claim that all instances of receiving and recounting predictions are merely parables, and therefore all share the title "Parable Chapter" (Piyu-pin), then the subsequent passages where there are likewise instances of receiving and recounting predictions throughout the three cycles of teaching should also be titled "Parable Chapter. Why then are their chapter titles all different?
This ritual procedure continues until the end of the scripture; thus, one should know that this does not exclude the immediate application as the standard.
The commentary states: "The essence of the Dharma-body is also proclaimed through skillful means.

This clarifies that while the *tathatā* Dharma-body is realized solely through wisdom, it is now being proclaimed through verbal expression; therefore, it is said to be "proclaimed by skillful means."
The Commentary states: "As for 'manifesting that both self and others are held as precious':

'self' refers to the section on Devadatta, wherein the Tathāgata’s body acts as a king who, seeking the weighty Dharma, relinquishes his royal throne to transcribe this sutra. 'Others' refers to the many bodies of Prabhūtaratna."
It is because they desire to hear this sutra that they have come here from afar.
The commentary states: "The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma brings great merit and benefit;

fearing that sentient beings might harbor doubts and the like," refers to those who previously briefly slandered this sutra, or who repeatedly frowned and harbored uncertainty. "You should listen to what happens to such a person," and so forth, up to "none at all."

[This merit is equal to] many kalpas. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Rejoicing," it is said that the merit of the fiftieth person who hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and is able to rejoice in it exceeds that of the sentient beings in four hundred million nayutas of trichiliocosms mentioned previously.
They shall obtain the seven treasures of gold and silver, and furthermore, they shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.
Even as stated in the "Chapter on Not Slighting," by upholding this sutra, one attains the purification of the six sense faculties.

Moreover, in the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," it says that if anyone can give rise to even a single thought of sympathetic joy toward this sutra, I shall likewise bestow upon them the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Such meritorious matters are beyond measure.

Fearing that sentient beings might harbor doubts and think the Buddha’s words were false or deceptive, he manifested the mark of his tongue to demonstrate that these are true words. "Dying for the sake of upholding the sutra" means to die;
"casting aside body and life to propagate the sutra" means to sacrifice one's physical existence for the sake of spreading the teaching.
Sixth, regarding the explanation of the main text of the sutra: first, various traditions will be presented, followed by an exegesis based on the commentaries.

Readers should be aware that since the Dharma flowed eastward from the Han dynasty, the eminent masters and sages of successive generations have explained the sutras and treatises according to the literal text, without establishing formal sections or enumerating the number of phrases.
It was not until the time of Master Dao’an of Xiangyang during the Later Qin dynasty that...

Regarding the division into chapters and sections: it is said that regardless of whether a sutra is large or small, it is customarily divided into three parts—namely, the Introduction (Nidāna), the Main Body (Prakṛta), and the Dissemination (Pariṇāmana).

This is identical to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* by the Western Bodhisattva Yaśomitra. Thus we know that although the transmission to the East was distant, the paths of the eminent sages were in harmony.
Contemporaries referred to Master Dao’an as the Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta. Among them was a Daoist named Xi Zuochi, who was exceptionally...

Regarding his learning and talent: Having heard that Master Dao’an was profoundly learned in both Buddhist and secular classics and possessed unimpeded eloquence, Xi Zuochi knocked on the gate and announced himself, saying, "Xi Zuochi from the four seas has come specifically to see you.
Thereupon, Master Dao’an sent someone to reply, "The monk Shi Dao’an, who covers the heavens, will see you shortly.
Since he described himself as one who "covers the heavens," it was even more grand than "the four seas. Once he came out to meet him...
Master Dao’an was walking ahead when the Xi family mocked him, saying, "Sifting it up and winnowing it out, the chaff and husks come first.
Master Dao’an replied, "Washing it with waves and rinsing it away, the sand and stones remain behind. On another day, Master Dao’an went to the garden pond of the Xi family.
The Xi family mocked him, saying, "O rabbit, rabbit, what do you seek as you come? Master Dao’an responded, "I have specifically come to look for a goat's head. The Xi family spoke again.
"Is the razor clean and ready for use? Master An replied, "I have already granted permission; it is fitting that the hair be left.
Other matters are as recounted in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan). Jizang divides [the scripture] into three sections. The introductory section is common to all [versions].

As for the main body (*zhengzong*), from the "Expedient Means" chapter up to the "Emergence from the Earth" chapter, it clarifies the provisional vehicle and the ultimate vehicle. From... [text continues]

In the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*, up to the middle of the *Guṇaparikīrtana-parivarta*, at the end of the initial section on the comparison of merits—consisting of one prose passage and one verse—it is stated:
"The merit of hearing this *āyuṣpramāṇa* and believing and understanding it is immeasurable. The above text clarifies the provisional and the ultimate.
Regarding the provisional and the real: that which attained the Unsurpassed Way beneath the Bodhi tree in the past was the provisional transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

As the Sūtra says, "Since I attained the Way," and so forth. Having passed through three incalculable *kalpas*, the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*) were already fully perfected.
This is the true *saṃbhogakāya*. Through the provisional and the real, it may be known. Thus, the "vehicle" (*yāna*) is the vehicle that conveys;
the "body" (*kāya*) is the body realized. The vehicle is the cause of realization, and the body is the fruit of realization. Therefore, [this is explained] by means of fifteen chapters and a half.

This is called the "Correct Main Body" (zhengzong). For example, in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányú jīng*), associating with virtuous friends constitutes the introductory section (*xiufen*).

Hearing the true Dharma and reflecting upon it according to principle constitute the correct main body. Practicing in accordance with the Dharma constitutes the dissemination section (*liútōng*). Furthermore, this may give rise to the three types of wisdom (*sanhui*).

Therefore, three sections are required. The introductory section (nidāna) causes the arising of wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth; it may also be divided into three according to the three faculties (*indriya*).

The introduction is for those of superior faculty, as they produce understanding immediately upon seeing [the teaching]. The main body (dharmakāya) is for those of middling faculty, as they only realize it through detailed and formal exposition.

The dissemination section (pariṇāmanā) is for those of inferior faculty, as they only comprehend and understand it after the teaching has been repeated three times. Furthermore, there are three conditions for its arrival [in this world].
Therefore, it is divided into three sections. The Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha, following the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, opens these three sections as follows:

first, the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching (*nidāna*); second, the section on the actual exposition of the teaching; and third, the section on practicing in accordance with the teaching.

Alternatively, the introduction may be understood as removing doubts and generating faith, the main body as destroying attachments to bring about understanding, and the circulation as practicing in accordance with the Dharma. At this time...

Regarding the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*), there are two interpretations; within these, there is yet another interpretation, making three interpretations in total. First, the first eight chapters constitute the *mūlaprakaraṇa* (the main body).

From the "Expedient Means" chapter (*upāyakauśalya-parivarta*) to the "Bestowal of Predictions upon Learners and Non-learners" chapter (*śaikṣāśaikṣavyākaraṇa-parivarta*), the One Vehicle prediction is specifically taught for those of the three faculties;
therefore, this is the main body. Second, from the "Expedient Means" chapter up to the midpoint of the "Dharma-preacher" chapter (*dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*)...

This constitutes the Main Teaching (*samyak-siddhānta*). Furthermore, because it bestows the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) upon the eight classes of beings, there is a specific intention within this section.
That is to say, at the beginning of the "Expedient Means" chapter, two kinds of profundity were revealed, stating that these matters cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the like.

Consequently, the assembly of śrāvakas and others all gave rise to doubt and confusion. Now, these eight chapters are intended to dispel those prior doubts; therefore, the bestowal of predictions is established as the Main Teaching.
Regarding the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta* as the main body (*śāsanamūla*) of the teaching: this is also stated in the verses of the *Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta*:
"Neither the devas nor the people of the world, nor any class of sentient beings, can know the Buddha. This means that those of the five vehicles and all sentient beings alike are unable to know him.
Now, at the beginning of this *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*, for the sake of all sentient beings—the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of supernatural beings, humans, and [the five...]—[the Buddha speaks].
The "Receiving of Prophecies" (*jìshòu jì*) constitutes the main body of the teaching (*zhèngzōng*), as it resolves the aforementioned doubts; thus it may also be termed the "Main Body.

The remaining nineteen chapters are termed the "Circulation Section" (*liúttòngfēn*). Regarding the third interpretation: from the "Expedient Means" chapter (*fāngbiàn pǐn*) up to the "Never-Despising" chapter (*chángbùqīng pǐn*), it is called the Main Body;

from the "Supernatural Powers" chapter (*shénlì pǐn*) onwards, it is the Circulation Section, as can be seen in the commentary (*shū*). Master Jing [the *Jìngfǎshī*] considers the nineteen chapters...

Regarding what constitutes the main body of the teaching: this refers to the section of the treatise that explains the seven similes, the three vehicles, and so forth. Upon reaching the "Life Span" chapter, the three vehicles and other such elements no longer appear;
they only reach their conclusion in the "Never Disparaging" chapter, as there is nothing of the sort thereafter. Thus, it may be known that this constitutes the main body of the teaching.

The Commentary states: "If this is so, then the former Master Zun was indeed a guiding light. Furthermore, there were two laymen, Liu Xin (read as *mào lín*) and his son Liu Bai, who would always use brushes, ink, and paper as tablets for their battles of debate; how much more so regarding the profound treasury of the Dharma?
These 'princes of the four seas,' who each took it upon themselves to act with mastery in their own time, found nothing in the commentaries and phrases that they did not refute."

The Preface states: "Master Jizang takes the fifteen chapters and a half beginning from the 'Expedient Means' chapter as the primary teaching (*zhengzong*), because they clarify the provisional and real aspects of the vehicle and the person.

Furthermore, he includes the prose section and one verse from the first half of the 'Distinguishing Merits' chapter, as these both record the great assembly hearing the Tathāgata’s discourse on the long duration of his life-span and the benefits obtained by sentient beings."

Regarding the title "The Correct Teaching" (*zhengzong*): If that is so, why is it that one obtains benefit not only by hearing the "Chapter on the Merits of Discernment," but from the "Chapter on Expedient Means" through to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra," where it is stated that bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in a trichiliocosm attain hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *dhāraṇīs* of revolution,
and are able to practice the path of Samantabhadra, and so forth in each successive chapter?

All [of these] contain benefit. That is to say, the former Master Zun stated that from the first chapter, titled "Preface," down to the end of the sutra, everything says it is beneficial and serves as a guide.
Now, regarding the Master Dao’s commentary, this objection is not necessarily correct.

According to the intention of Master Zhenzang, those who obtain benefit within the True Teaching do so precisely because they hear of the abandonment of the three [vehicles] for the sake of the One and thereby receive a prediction of enlightenment.

Śrāvakas derive benefit from this; although the benefit is the same, the hearing of the Dharma differs for each. That which is benefited by means of the One Vehicle is termed the "Correct Doctrine" (saddharma);
that which is benefited by means other than the One Vehicle is termed the "Circulation" (pravartana). How could this contradict the principle? (And so forth.)

The Commentary states: "To praise, certify, receive the mandate, and entrust [the teaching] so that it may be practiced" refers to the interpretation of the names of the nineteen chapters as the *pariṇāmanā-vibhāga* (section on the dissemination).
This explains the *Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*; within that chapter, the person and the Dharma are praised and revered because they serve as models for study. This accounts for two chapters.
This refers to the "Chapter on Seeing the Jeweled Stūpa," the "Chapter on Devadatta," and the "Chapter on Encouraging Faith," which serve as the proof that the teachings are not false.

Furthermore, eight chapters are explained according to their assigned roles: the "Chapter on Upholding," the "Chapter on Peaceful Practices," the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth," the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Lifespan," the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits," the "Chapter on the Merits of Rejoicing," the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," and the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never Disparaging."

Sā. These eight chapters were all received and propagated by command. As for the two chapters on "Entrustment"—the "Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power" chapter and the "Entrustment" chapter—they involve the earnest entrustment so that [the teaching] may circulate. Thus, there are six ways in which it is put into practice.

Regarding the statement that "explaining the objects [of cognition] causes one to know the provisional and the real of the vehicles": this refers to explaining the words of the teaching that serves as the expressive medium (*vyañjana*), thereby revealing the principle that is expressed (*artha*).

This causes all listeners to take those words and their meanings as mental objects. Since these words and their meanings are the objects of the conscious mind, they constitute both the teaching and the principle.
Since one has already recognized the right and wrong of the vehicles, one abandons the provisional and adopts the real.

To "expound the practice so as to make known the right and wrong of the causes" means to expound the true cause of the One Vehicle, thereby causing one to abandon the provisional practices of the Two Vehicles.
Regarding the teaching on the fruit that causes one to know the true transformation of the body, and so forth, up to the manifestation of the supreme virtues accomplished through cause and fruit:
from the *Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* to the five chapters of the *Sadāparibhūta*, the teaching on the fruit causes one to know the true transformation of the body.

This refers to those such as the followers of the Two Vehicles who cling to the notion that the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, [mistaking] the *saṃbhogakāya* for all that was realized.

Liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are taken as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Following the forms of the six realms of existence to teach and transform sentient beings is called the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Furthermore, in this sutra, when various bodhisattvas emerged from the earth and the followers of the two vehicles all gave rise to doubt, saying that these were not the Buddha's transformations, the Buddha extensively explained in the "Chapter on the Lifespan" how he departed from the palace of the Śākya clan.
Not far from the city of Gayā, beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

From his birth in the royal palace through the eight phases of attaining the Way and so forth—these are the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), which is precisely what makes known the transformation of the body.

Furthermore, it is said that since my attainment of Buddhahood, an exceedingly long time has passed; the span of my life is even greater than that number, and I have always remained on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Furthermore, the fact that other dwelling places are constantly filled with devas and humans refers to the reality of the body.

As for the fruit of its realization, it is the "Chapter on Lifespan," which clarifies the longevity of life and the long-term attainment of Buddhahood; this is the cause of realization, namely the four subsequent chapters.

The sections on "Distinguishing Merits," "Rejoicing," "The Dharma Master," and "Never-Disparaging" encourage one to recognize the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and seek realization of the true body (*dharmakāya*).

To cause one to recognize that [the Buddha] beneath the Bodhi tree is the transformation body, and to seek realization of the true, is to cause one to practice the causes of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and to attain the fruit of the One Vehicle; this is precisely the fruit of the long-lasting *dharmakāya* of the Lifespan [Chapter] (and so forth).
However, there are five categories of persons who obtain benefit therein: first, those with faith; second, those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [the text];
third, those who explain it for others; fourth, those who concurrently practice the six perfections. These five types of persons are able to accomplish supreme merit (and so forth).
Regarding the phrase "gradually attaining the two supreme virtues of cause and fruit": this refers to cause and fruit within the state of the cause; therefore, it is called "gradual attainment.
If these were in the state of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhaphala*), they would have already been fully perfected and attained, and thus could not be called "gradual attainment.
As for "cause and fruit within the cause," there is the cause within the cause, the fruit within the cause, the fruit within the fruit, and the cause within the fruit. First, [the author] says:

Regarding the causes within the causes: these include the exhortations to uphold the sutra and so forth in the "Chapter on Merit" (*Guṇaparyāya*), and the rejoicing performed by the fiftieth person and others in the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā*).

These are all causes within the causes. Regarding the fruits within the causes: these consist of attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), obtaining enlightenment after four or three births, and even being able to turn the pure wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). These are the merits of rejoicing.
Within this chapter, by rejoicing in and hearing [this teaching], one will always obtain a handsome countenance and be endowed with all the marks of a superior person;

furthermore, one will obtain celestial palaces and so forth. Even in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," it is stated that upholding, reciting, and so forth this sutra constitutes the cause, which enables the attainment of six thousand merits and the like—these are termed the fruit. All of these are instances of cause and effect within the context of the causal stage.

Regarding "the cause within the fruit": this refers to the cause-and-fruit relationship within the aforementioned cause; it is the cultivation of the cause while carrying the fruit, and is collectively termed "the cause within the fruit.
The *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit is termed "the fruit within the fruit. Regarding "the superior virtues of the two stages":

these refer to the fruit within the cause, which is precisely the fruit within the fruit. Furthermore, there is the "already perfected fruit," namely the *Tathāgata-āyus-pramāṇa-parivarta*. [The text continues: "not yet..."
"Full fruition" refers to the merit of rejoicing (*anumodanā*) and so forth, all of which are fruits within the causal stage.
"The Bodhisattva knows this and thereby realizes the Path" means that those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] from among the two vehicles and beyond are all termed "Bodhisattvas.
"Realizing the Path" refers to the various Bodhisattvas mentioned in the "Chapter on the Merit of Rejoicing," some of whom are in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

This refers to such things as attaining enlightenment in two or three lifetimes. If one discusses the sequence of cultivation and realization in terms of cause preceding effect, it is called "cause and effect.

If one discusses the sequence of manifesting cultivation in terms of effect preceding cause, it is called "effect and cause. This means that by first presenting the result, one causes [the practitioner] to aspire to cultivation;
thus, it is called "the cause for realizing the result. It fully reveals the sublime virtues accomplished through this effect-and-cause relationship.
This serves as a summary of the preceding meaning. From the "Chapter on Lifespan" up to the "Chapter on Never-Disparaging," the superior virtues of cause and effect have already been clarified;
there is no other intention [beyond this]. The eight chapters from here downward are called the "Propagation Section" (and so forth).

The Commentary states: "Regarding 'manifesting signs, entrusting, and receiving the mandate to practice': 'Manifesting signs' refers to the *Śakti-vyākaraṇa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Manifestation of Spiritual Power), which means that the Tathāgata extends his broad and long tongue up to the Brahma-heaven to signify that his words are not false; thus, it is called manifesting signs.

'Entrusting' refers to the *Parīndanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Entrustment), which is exemplified by [the Buddha] using his golden hand to stroke the crown of the Bodhisattva's head. 'Receiving the mandate to practice' refers to..."
In the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta" and at the end of the sutra, the entrustment for its circulation through distant ages is received. Within this circulation, there are further three parts.
The first consists of the chapters from "The Dharma Master" to "Ratnāvatī," which constitutes the circulation of direct realization (*pratyakṣa-prasāra*).

The second consists of seven chapters: "Peaceful Conduct," "Emergence," "Life Span," "Distinction," "Rejoicing," "The Dharma Master," and "Not Disparaging," which constitutes the circulation of practice and study.

The eight chapters from "Supernatural Powers" (*Ṛddhi*) onwards constitute the entrustment and circulation (*parindanā-pracāra*). According to the introduction to the *Śāstra*, up to the point where it enumerates the seven kinds of accomplishment (*siddhi*), these should be correlated with the treatise as can be understood from the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The commentary states: "Regarding 'the seer illuminates the object to be illuminated,' 'the illuminator' refers to light, and 'the illuminated' refers to the seven things within that light (and so forth).
The commentary further states:
"The perfection of the mountain city symbolizes its superiority over other sūtras, which receive the title of 'preface' only partially; [for here], all seven kinds of accomplishment are complete."
This is the introduction. How is it that these two alone receive their respective names? The answer is: the wise attain understanding through analogies.
For example, among those who travel in the world, everyone after they have left their door is a traveler; yet only the one who is currently on the road receives the name "traveler.

Again, for example, among those attending a banquet, whether for auspicious or inauspicious occasions, all are guests; however, if one is attending a funeral, one cannot be called a "guest" [in the formal sense]. Furthermore, it is like this: [the rest of the analogy follows].

The names of the plants are the same; however, *shu-yu* (the grain) alone receives the name of the plant itself. Likewise, regarding the "ten minds of faith," these are the ten types beginning with faith.
If one discusses the ten types as they are, they are all forms of faith; yet, it is only faith itself that specifically receives the name "faith."
Furthermore, it is like the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Because the eye can see form (*rūpa*), it is called an "object" (*viṣaya*);

yet the other [objects], such as sound, fragrance, and so forth, are also forms and are also objects, yet they do not receive the name "form. Only that which is seen by the eye specifically receives the designation "form. This mountain city is also like this:

although it is generally called an "introduction" (*nidāna*), these two [the mountain and the city] specifically receive the name "introduction. Moreover, among the seven factors of accomplishment (*saptasamudāgama*), [this is the case].

There are two reasons why this is not found in other sūtras: first, it is absent from the Hīnayāna sūtras; second, it is absent from those Mahāyāna sūtras that do not manifest the ten kinds of causes through Mañjuśrī.
Question: Since the *Warm Bath Sūtra* (*Oṣadhikāra-sūtra*), the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and others all mention mountain cities, why is this sūtra alone designated as supreme?
Answer: This sūtra explains the principles of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), which are subtle, wondrous, and profoundly deep, thereby reconciling provisional means back to the ultimate truth.
Indeed, [the Buddha] extensively bestows predictions upon them. Furthermore, there is the presence of the Many-Jeweled Stūpa to certify this sutra, as well as its entrustment for circulation;
all of these are matters of the bodhisattva’s practice, unlike other sutras, and thus it alone is distinguished as supreme.
Regarding the initial term "Introduction" (nidāna), there have been four traditional interpretations handed down from antiquity: first, the "Inception"; second, the "Testimony of Faith.
As for the Testimony of Faith, it refers to the six phrases at the beginning of this sutra, such as "Thus have I heard," and so forth.

Ānanda cites himself and others as witnesses, attesting that he personally heard [the teaching] from the Buddha, thereby providing testimony for this sutra and causing others to give rise to faith. Second, the "Inception Sequence" (nidāna-nidāna) is as follows:
When he was about to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he first preached for the bodhisattvas a Mahāyāna sūtra titled the *Anantārtha*.

This served as the introductory inspiration through such events as the falling of flowers from the sky and the sixfold trembling of the earth. When he preached the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, after entering the city to beg for food and washing his feet, this served as the introductory inspiration.
In the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, five hundred parasols were joined together to form a single parasol, and this foul [city] was transformed.

He then regarded it as a pure land and took it as his point of departure. When the time for preaching the *Nirvāṇa* arrived, on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the hour of dawn while chewing a willow twig, the World-Honored One uttered a great sound, universally proclaiming throughout the trichiliocosm:
"The Tathāgata shall enter *nirvāṇa* this very night. If you have any doubts, you should consult me regarding what you wish to ask; this is the final [opportunity]."
The subsequent questions and so forth serve as the introduction (as explained at length). Regarding the second interpretation: first, the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) is clarified;

next, the specific introduction (*pratyeka-nidāna*) is clarified. An ancient commentator explained: "Thus have I heard" and the following two phrases constitute the general introduction, because they are common to all sūtras.

"At one time" and what follows constitute the specific introduction, which specifies the time, place, and the assembly of followers—both monastics and laypeople, comprising the eight classes of beings. As for their number...

Regarding the measure of their number: because each is distinct. According to Master Jiguang, these six phrases extend from the beginning up until the point where "at that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who offered him worship, respect, honor, and praise."

This is the general introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*). Although it differs from other sūtras regarding the number of the assembly, it is considered the general introduction because it possesses six common phrases.

The scriptural text from "having sat cross-legged" (*paryaṅkam ābhujya*) onwards is called the specific introduction (*viśeṣanidāna*), because the manifestation of auspicious signs and the emission of light differ in their characteristics.

Alternatively, the section up to "retreating to sit on one side" may be the general introduction, while the section beginning with "at that time, the World-Honored One" is the specific introduction. Third.

Regarding the "explanation": first is the introduction by Ānanda; second is the introduction by the Tathāgata, such as "Thus have I heard" and so forth. That which emerges from Ānanda is called the introduction by Ānanda.
That which precedes the preaching of this sutra—such as the falling of flowers and the shaking of the earth—is called the introduction by the Tathāgata.

A fourth explanation concerns the introduction to the True Sutra and the introduction to the Image Sutra. "True" refers to when the Buddha was in the world and first preached the Mahāyāna for the sake of the various bodhisattvas.

The sūtras and so forth are such examples. Regarding the "preface to the sūtra" (sūtra-nidāna): it refers to the six phrases, beginning with "Thus have I heard," which Ānanda himself spoke when the various arhats were compiling the Dharma-piṭaka after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
This is also called the "preface before the sūtra" (pūrva-nidāna) and the "postface after the sūtra" (paścāt-nidāna).
This is the postscript to this sutra, which precedes the preface to this sutra. Furthermore, the preface to this sutra follows the postscript to this sutra;
that is to say, Ānanda’s preface stands after the Tathāgata’s preface.

Next, I shall explain the six phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard. Regarding the various interpretations and expositions by scholars of antiquity, there are numerous schools of thought differing in how they expand or condense these phrases.
Herein, I shall briefly outline their number. First, those who expand them into eight phrases are as follows:
"Thus" (1), "I" (2), "heard" (3), "time" (4), "Buddha" (5), "dwelling in the royal city" (6), "mountain" (7), and "assembly" (8); these together constitute eight.

Second, according to the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha, this is explained as seven phrases: first, "thus" (evam), referring to the Dharma that was heard; second, "I" (aham), referring to the person who heard it;
third, "heard" (śrutam), meaning to have personally received the words and intent; fourth, "at one time" (ekasmin samaye), referring to the occasion when the teaching was given;

fifth, "Buddha," referring to the teacher who expounded the doctrine; sixth, "dwelling at Śrāvastī," referring to the location where the teaching was given; and seventh, "together with a great assembly of bhikṣus," etc.

The third [element], the disciples to be converted (*vineya*). Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Great Commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom) to explain the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* by resolving it into six points:
first, the Dharma as heard; second, "I have heard," referring to the person who hears; third, "at one time," the time of the teaching’s delivery; fourth, "Buddha," the teacher of the doctrine;
fifth, the "dwelling place"; and sixth, the disciples to be converted. Ratnaprabhā Bodhisattva composed the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-vṛtti*.
If one discusses this according to the *Śāstra*, it also consists of six points, identical to those in Nāgārjuna’s treatise. He himself stated: "The first three clarify the disciples;
the latter three testify to the Teacher's exposition. This is the case for all sūtras. Fourth is the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu.

Based on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* was composed, explaining [the sūtra] through five phrases: first, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), which manifests one's own capacity to hear;
second, the time; third, the Buddha; fourth, the dwelling place; and fifth, the disciples to be converted. Regarding the fifth [phrase], I shall now explain it myself through four points:
first, "Thus," "at one time," and so forth, all of which pertain to the Dharma; second, "I heard" and "the assembly of bhikṣus," which clarify the capacity [to hear].
"Thus have I heard. These [referring to the assembly] are the Saṃgha. "The Buddha" refers to the Buddha himself. "The four matters" refers to the dwelling place.
The sixth [section], the Sautrāntika masters, following the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, explain it as three phrases: namely, Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha. The Buddha is the Buddha-jewel.
