Likewise, those who were staying at one time in places such as the royal city or the mountains are the Dharma-jewel. "Thus have I heard" and "the great assembly of bhikṣus," and so forth, constitute the Saṃgha.
Treasure. Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The Three Jewels are most auspicious; thus they are spoken of at the beginning of my sutras.
Seventh, there are only two phrases, namely: persons and the Dharma. "I have heard" and "the assembly of bhikṣus," etc., refer to persons; the remainder refers to the Dharma.
Alternatively, these may be taken as a single phrase, all being subsumed under the Dharma. Or again, there may be no single phrase at all, which is to say:
They return to suchness. Therefore, the subsequent sutra states that all dharmas are quiescent and have the characteristic of quiescence, as proclaimed by the ultimate words.

As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "Since I attained the Way more than forty years ago, I have not uttered a single word therein. Vimalakīrti also said: "As for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstration;
as for those who listen to the Dharma, there is no hearing and no attainment. Thus, one knows that there is no preaching and no...
This is called "expounding the Dharma. According to the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* cited below, it says: "Those who have not yet expounded the Dharma are like the leaves in a forest;
those who have already expounded the Dharma are like a single drop in the ocean. This is precisely what should be explained, and it must be interpreted as follows.
Master Yan’s commentary on the six phrases states: "Three phrases possess both words and meaning; three phrases possess meaning but lack words. That is to say: [text continues]
The three phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard at one time" were spoken by the Buddha himself; they possess both meaning and verbal expression.

From the words "The Buddha was staying at... onwards, there is only the meaning but no specific verbal expression, because at that time the World-Honored One did not explicitly state the direction, location, or the number of the assembly (and so forth).

Regarding the origin of this teaching: it refers to when [the Buddha], being about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, addressed the great assembly at large, saying, "Tonight, I shall definitively enter *parinirvāṇa*.
If you have any doubts, you should freely ask whatever you wish; let this be your final question.

Ānanda, remaining in the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*), had not yet eliminated his afflictions and did not realize that this was a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); he spoke as if it were a true extinction. Therefore, his mind was again filled with grief and regret.

Unable to overcome his grief, Aniruddha and Upāli then said to Ānanda, "The Tathāgata exists today, yet he will not exist tomorrow. If you have any doubts, why do you not ask the Buddha about them? Ānanda replied:
"I am now deluded and frantic; I do not know what to ask. Thereupon, Ānanda posed four questions as recorded in the commentary.
The Buddha replied: "After my parinirvāṇa, the Prātimokṣa shall be your great teacher.
It will be no different whether I am in the world or after my passing; in both cases, one must act in accordance with the precepts. One should rely upon the precepts."
It is for the sake of being a teacher. *Prātimokṣa* is here translated as "the precepts that accord with liberation.
If one can firmly uphold these prohibitive precepts, one will be able to accord with and reach liberation. Regarding the second question, "Upon what should one rely for dwelling?

one should dwell relying upon the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. Within these four, there are generally three types of contemplation according to their superior, middling, and inferior [capacities]. First:
There are three types of contemplation: contemplation of provisional characteristics, contemplation of two matters, and contemplation of principle.

Regarding "contemplation of provisional characteristics," this refers to contemplating the impurity of the body, which is a provisional combination of the four great elements and is composed of thirty-six constituent parts.

It is like a bag filled with filth and excrement, intended to make the disciples realize that their bodies are formed by outflows and afflictions; thus, they are deeply loathsome and defiled, and are termed the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).

Second, regarding the contemplation that sensation is suffering: it causes one to know that the triple world is a burning house where there is no place to hide the body, and that one is being scorched day and night by the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.
To be able to contemplate in this way is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Third, regarding the contemplation that the mind is impermanent:

it recognizes that the consciousness-mind undergoes constant transformation and does not abide for even a single moment. It causes one to know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no permanent abiding, thereby leading one to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Therefore, [it is] *nirvāṇa*.

The *Pǎn jīng* (Brahmajāla-sūtra) says: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent... down to: Nirvana is bliss. Regarding the fourth contemplation, the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), the verse from the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states:
"The Buddhas sometimes speak of a self, and sometimes speak of non-self; yet within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All phenomena lack the characteristic of a self, up to and including the characteristic of a life-principle (*jīvātmaka*)."
If one clings to the notion that there is a self within the dharmas, the Tathāgata says such a person is not a bodhisattva.

One who practices this contemplation is able to realize the principle of the two kinds of selflessness; this is called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Why did the World-Honored One instruct [beings] to practice the contemplation of the provisional?
It is because sentient beings do not know that this body is fundamentally false and deceptive, and that their delusions are unreal; therefore, he teaches them...
My disciples should constantly practice the contemplation of the provisional. After my parinirvāṇa, you should always abide by this. Regarding the second matter, the contemplation of phenomena:
one divides the four foundations of mindfulness into the five aggregates. First, the body is the aggregate of form; one contemplates that form is impure.

Next, sensation is the aggregate of feeling; one contemplates that feeling is suffering. People of the world give rise to the perception of pleasure even within lower forms of suffering. This is not so.
Know that both the two sensations of suffering and pleasure are entirely suffering. Pleasure is a provisional sensation;

even if one enjoys the wondrous fruits of reward in the realms of humans and devas, once that retribution is exhausted, one cannot escape impermanence. The sensation of suffering is real. Therefore, the sutra below states: "The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is real and without variation.
The *Śāriputraśāsanopadeśa* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) says: "The sun may be made cold, the moon may be made hot, but what the Buddha has taught as suffering [remains as it is]."

The truths cannot be made pleasant. The three factors constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which brings about the knowledge that all phenomena are impermanent from moment to moment.

The four mental states constitute the aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which bring about the knowledge that mind and consciousness are fundamentally without self (*anātman*).

If one does not bind oneself to objects of focus and does not abide in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), yet claims, "I am capable of this, while others are not," it is like a monkey.
A monkey that has found a tree; a mad elephant without a hook; a wild horse without a tether; a bull whose nose-string is severed—this is called the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*).
Third, the contemplation of the true principle (*tattva-vipaśyanā*) corresponds solely to the principle and is free from further objective conceptualization.

All five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) ultimately return to emptiness and are of one single *dharmatā*. Therefore, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* says: "O Bodhi..."
When the Bodhisattva practices the profound *prajñā*, he perceives that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, thereby crossing over all suffering and calamity;
this is called contemplation of principle (*li-guan*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are five kinds of impurity by which the body is formed:
first, impurity of the dwelling place, which refers to the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*), which for nine months constantly resides below the mother’s stomach and above her large intestine.
It is placed above [the ground] by the side of a pit for urine and excrement; thus, a verse from a sutra says: "This body is foul and impure;
it is not born from flowers, nor from *campaka* blossoms, nor is it born from fruit"—this refers to that very matter.
Second, regarding the impurity of the seed: since beginningless time, the *ālaya-vijñāna* has accumulated as the cause, driven by the winds of karma.
Blown [into existence], these seeds of consciousness rely upon and grasp the red and white vital essences of the parents to form a body;
therefore, it is called "impure. As a verse says: "The seed of this body is impure; it is not some other wondrous treasure. It does not arise from that which is pure and white."
It merely emerges from a foul passage. Third, regarding the impurity of the three intrinsic natures (*trisvabhāva*):
this refers to the thirty-six substances covered by a thin skin, filled within with various forms of excrement and filth; this is called "impurity. As a verse says:

"The elements of earth, water, fire, and wind can transform into impurity; even if one were to empty the ocean to wash this body, it could not be made fragrant and clean. Fourth, the [four] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the state of impurity: it refers to the constant flow from the nine orifices. From the eyes come rheum and tears; from the ears, wax; from the nose, mucus;
from the mouth, saliva and spittle; and from the passages of excretion, feces and urine flow forth.
Though fine clothes adorn the exterior and delicious food fills the interior, they all become impure. As a verse says: "Various kinds of impure things fill the body within. Constantly...
The outflows ceaselessly flow forth, like a leaking bag filled with things. Regarding the five ultimate impurities:
after one has passed away, this defiled body becomes dung for worms and wolves, ash when fire is set to it, and earth when it decays and rots;
thus it is impure. As a verse says: "Examine this body with discernment; it will ultimately return to the place of death. It is difficult to restrain..."

It is thus that [the body] repeatedly turns away from its benefactors as if they were unseen. Therefore, one should know that although it was once adorned with fine ointments, it will inevitably return to stench and filth;

and although it was extensively decorated with silks and ornaments, it will all return to decay and extinction. Thus, the verse of admonition by an Arhat to the King says: "The eyes are holes for rheum and tears; the nose is a pouch for foul snot;
the mouth is a vessel for saliva and spittle; the body is a storehouse for excrement and urine. O Great King, there is nothing [to be gained here]."
"I understand. You have been corrupted by sensual desires. I, this poor monk, possess the eye of wisdom; I have left the household life to seek the site of enlightenment. Third:
When a bhikṣu of evil character is dealt with according to the *brahmadanda*, "Brahma" refers to the Brahma Heaven, and this is the Dharma. "Danda" means the application of the Dharma.

If there is a bhikṣu who is of evil character and arrogant, he should be dealt with according to the pure Dharma; there is no need for beating or scolding—rather, he is to be expelled through silent treatment (*tūṣṇīka-pravāsanīya*).

Furthermore, as for the fourth point regarding what words should be placed [at the beginning]: at the head of all sūtras, one should always place the six phrases beginning with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), which constitute the causal origin (*nidāna*) of the compilation.
Regarding the basis for this establishment: according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, such a person possesses the characteristic of faith (*śraddhā*).

Why is it that faith is mentioned at the very outset? According to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, faith has five kinds of functions (*karman*): first, its function is to eliminate lack of faith. Once one has faith in the Buddha-dharma, one’s reverence becomes profound;
even if one encounters adverse conditions, one’s faith will certainly not waver. Second, its function is to bring about common benefit. First, for oneself...
Subsequently, it causes others who lack faith to likewise eliminate [their lack of faith]. Because it eliminates [the lack of faith] in others, it causes [faith] to arise.

A secular text says: "What you do not desire for yourself, do not inflict upon others. Therefore, one must first possess faith. Third, its function is to serve as the provision (*sambhāra*) for attaining *bodhi*;

this refers to the initial stage of faith among the forty stages of mind (*cittotpāda*). Fourth, its function is to enable progress toward the good realms; that is, by attaining the four kinds of indestructible faith (*aveccappasāda*), one is able to transcend [the lower realms].
The evil realms. If a person lacks faith, it increases ignorance (*moha*). Fifth, its function is to increase pure faith.
If one lacks faith, the mind is largely turbid; since faith alone [purifies], the nature must necessarily be clear.
Therefore, know that having faith without wisdom increases ignorance, such that one cannot discern right from wrong. Due to this ignorance, one gives rise to false faith.
Furthermore, if one possesses wisdom but lacks faith, it will increase wrong views; that is, worldly cleverness and eloquence will increase heterodox perspectives.
Therefore, this faith also takes wrong wisdom as its essential nature. Moreover, there are four meanings: first, to establish faith by ceasing doubt.
Fearing that future sentient beings might doubt whether the *Sūtras* were spoken by the Buddha, [the phrase] "Thus" (*evam*) was placed [at the beginning] to resolve such uncertainty.
1. To dispel doubts. 2. To destroy attachments so as to engender faith. When there is attachment, one does not understand;

thus, by destroying that attachment, one causes faith and understanding to arise. 3. To cease other forms of slander. If it were said that these were spoken by others, many might give rise to slander;
now, by saying that Ānanda heard them directly from the Buddha, people immediately develop faith. 4. To rectify wrong views. At the beginning of the scriptures of non-Buddhists...
Both are the two characters *a* and *nā*. They are considered auspicious because the beginning is auspicious; therefore, the middle and the end are also auspicious.
*A* means "non-existence" (*abhāva*), and *nā* means "existence" (*bhāva*). All phenomena do not depart from these two characters, existence and non-existence;
therefore, they were placed at the beginning. Now, to refute false views, they are placed thus. Furthermore, there are two kinds of faith: the faith of a Bodhisattva is profound and...
It is not shallow, because they are free from doubt. Although they have attained the wisdom and principle of the two kinds of emptiness, they still desire to attain unexcelled Bodhi;
therefore, the sutra below states: "Except for those Bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm, there will certainly be no regression.

Next, as for those of the Two Vehicles, they are shallow and not deep. Although it is said that they possess the wisdom and principle of the emptiness of persons, they seek only the small fruit and regress midway.
They turn back and are unable to advance further to seek the Mahāyāna. Therefore, the Sūtra below says:
"If we were to hear of purifying Buddha-lands and teaching sentient beings, we would have no joy or delight whatsoever. Third, ordinary persons are neither deep nor shallow;
they arise whenever they encounter conditions, like floating duckweed. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Ordinary persons are like light feathers, following the wind."
Moving east and west, one cannot abide in stillness. A secular poem says: "The traveler’s heart has no fixed place; it is like an unmoored boat. It also says:
"Life is like a drop of dew," meaning there is no certainty—this refers to that very matter. Furthermore, a book records:
"Yanling returned the sword to the withered pine," and Yuan Baqin offered a slaughtered chicken as a token of his pledge. They met across a thousand li, punctually according to their appointment.

...and thus arrive. This is to preserve one's trustworthiness (*xin*). Therefore, among benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness, that which is listed last is intended to be practiced first.
Furthermore, the *xingxing* can speak but does not depart from the category of beasts; the parrot can speak but does not depart from the category of birds.
If a person lacks trustworthiness, though they possess speech, how do they differ from a bird? Thus the Master said: "One who serves their parents should be able to exhaust their..."

[He possesses] strength. When serving his ruler, he is able to place himself [rightly]; when associating with friends, his words are trustworthy. Although it is said that he has not yet studied, I must say of him: "He has studied.
Furthermore, regarding the initial statement, "Thus causing faith to arise," there are three meanings: first, to cause sentient beings to believe that this was spoken by the Buddha;
second, to believe that the Buddha-nature exists within their own bodies; and third, to believe that they will certainly attain realization in the future.

The Buddha indeed possesses such a meaning; therefore, it was placed at the beginning. Regarding Master Jing’s interpretation that "the mind's determination constitutes the essence of faith (*śraddhā*), while verbal determination constitutes its characteristic," this is not correct; the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) have been confused.
According to the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, that which is "determination" has resolute confidence (*adhimokṣa*) as its essence, whereas that which is "faith" has purity (*prasāda*) as its essence.
Therefore, we know this is an error. However, in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, [faith] is taken as having purity as its essence; because one possesses faith, the mind first realizes purity.
If one lacks faith, the mind becomes turbid, and upon encountering an object, it arises immediately; this takes false wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*) as its essence.
Alternatively, it may be said that faith takes provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "It has the capacity to attain the real."
Because the mind is pure: "that which truly exists" refers to the Four Noble Truths; "attainment" refers to faith in the Three Jewels; and "ability" refers to faith in supramundane wholesome dharmas.
Because one has faith in these three, it is called "purity of faith. Therefore, at the beginning of the sutra, it is stated thus:

the intention is to cause the arising of faith in these three dharmas. As for the later statement, "practicing in accordance with them so that wisdom may arise": once wisdom has arisen, this is why...

One should joyfully accept and practice this. Furthermore, it first causes faith to arise and makes that faith firm; subsequently, it causes wisdom to arise, whereby one immediately transcends birth and death.

Regarding the ten meanings of "faith" explained in the commentary, that which is the initial cause for proceeding toward the ultimate fruit refers to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). As for the "fruit":
Regarding the supreme fruit of unsurpassed bodhi, the initial cause consists of the forty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Because faith is primary at the beginning of the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*), it is called the "initial cause.

As for the ten virtues that must be possessed when first generating the great bodhicitta, the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* states: first, drawing near to virtuous friends; second, making offerings to all Buddhas; third, practicing...

1. Cultivating the roots of goodness; 2. Resolutely seeking the supreme Dharma; 3. A mind that is always gentle and supple; 4. Being able to endure suffering when encountered; 5. Having a profound and pure compassion;
6. A deep mind of equanimity; 7. Loving and delighting in the Mahāyāna; 8. Seeking the wisdom of the Buddha. Regarding the arousal of the three sublime contemplations:
the mind of weary detachment from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is the vow to sever all evil, which is the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). As for...
May all evil karma throughout the worlds of the ten directions, vast as space, be completely severed and exhausted.

This is also the cause for the *dharmakāya* within the three virtues (*triguṇa*), specifically the virtue of merit (*puṇyaguṇa*). Second is the seeking of the unsurpassed bodhicitta, which is the vow to cultivate all that is wholesome.
This is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). One vows to cultivate every single virtue throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as vast as space;
this is the cause of the wisdom-body (*jñāna-dharma-kāya*) and the cause of the reward-body (*vipāka-kāya*). Third, for the sake of delivering sentient beings, one vows to deliver all living beings;

this is called the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). One vows that all sentient beings existing within the worlds of the ten directions shall be delivered without exception.
This is called "gratitude" (*anugraha*), which is the cause for the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). Therefore, it is termed the "three sublime contemplations.

It is also the threefold pure precepts (*tri-śīla*) and the cause for the three bodies (*trikāya*). It brings to perfection the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The commentary (*ṭīkā*) quotes the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* as saying:
"The power of pure supremacy," etc. Here, "purity" refers to faith; as the commentary states, this is the "great bodhicitta," taking the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) as its basis.
The "intrinsic nature" refers to the purity of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). "Supreme power" refers to strong conditions;

the commentary states that this takes a virtuous friend as the condition. "Firm resolve for superior progress" refers to what the commentary calls "not retreating or yielding, but rather exerting oneself."
To "exert oneself" means that when one begins to advance toward the Way, even if there is regression or discouragement, one must immediately concentrate the mind in pursuit,
free from all other thoughts, and give rise to great vows to bind oneself by oath; this is the resolve and integrity of a practitioner among worldly people.
Regarding the second, those whose faculties for entering the principle of the truths are gradual, this refers to the virtues of the stage of application (*prayoga*).

For those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), upon attaining entry into the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the first fruit, they realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). For Bodhisattvas, while in the stage of application and about to enter the first ground (*bhūmi*), they will realize the principle of the two kinds of selflessness (*dharma-pudgala-nairātmya*).
To do so, one must first possess the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and five powers (*pañcabala*) within the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) before being able to realize it.
The wisdom of the two emptinesses is the beginning of the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), both of which possess the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).

Because there is the power of faith, all wholesome states, whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), arise from this basis. Because there is the power of faith, no māras can subdue them.

According to Master Bingzhou, it should be said that this is the "cry of entering the principle of the Truths" (*di-li zhi ming-jian*). As for the "cry of entering" (*ming-jian*), it is like the cry of a crane about to fly; at first...
One foot, two feet, up to ten feet, and even soaring toward the heavens. This soaring height is entirely due to the momentum of gradual flight.
That is to say, when those of the Great and Small Vehicles wish to enter the Noble Path, they must rely upon the faculty of faith and the power of faith regarding the fruit of Buddhahood;

only then can they enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). From the Path of Seeing, they enter the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); from the Path of Cultivation, they enter the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*). Thus...

Up until the attainment of Buddhahood, the causes for achieving Buddhahood all arise from the generation of faith; therefore, it is called the "Gradual Sound. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are at the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*);

the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) are at the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*); the five faculties (*indriya*) are at the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*); and the five powers (*bala*) are at the stage of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

According to the Mahāyāna school, the five faculties are at the stage of Heat, and the five powers are within the stages of Patience and the Supreme Worldly Dharma. This is the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
It is the foremost among the practices because it possesses the five faculties and the five powers. From this, all myriad virtues arise;
the four māras cannot cause harm, and one is finally able to enter the path of vision and realize suchness.

What is called "the penetration of the wondrous, true, and pure" refers precisely to the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*). "Penetration" means thorough understanding. "Wondrous" refers to wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*). "True" refers to suchness (*tathatā*).
"Pure" refers to the seven purities of faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, it arises from realizing this purity, wondrousness, suchness, and the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). Having entered the Path of Seeing, one is immediately able to develop pure faith in the Triple Gem and the precepts.
Now, these precepts are the "precepts beloved by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*), which are the precepts co-existent with the Path and co-existent with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This means that simply by generating pure faith toward the Triple Gem, the precepts of the Noble Path arise spontaneously. As the analogy in the treatise states: "The Buddha..."
The Jewel of the Buddha is like a physician; the Jewel of the Dharma is like a medicinal prescription; and the Jewel of the Sangha is like a nurse. It is not possible to lack even one of these.
May all sentient beings give rise to these three thoughts toward the Triple Gem. Through this, the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones will naturally increase.
Because the precepts increase, they will attain the sublime fruits of rebirth among humans and devas, which is precisely the cause for departing from poverty and low status. Therefore—

The initial statement "Thus" is intended to inspire faith (the four indestructible faiths, as explained in a separate commentary). However, within this sutra, the character for "purity" (*śuddha*) is not explicitly defined;
in the subsequent text, it merely mentions "becoming free from dust and defilement to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye. Yet, this is not the primary meaning.
Other passages state, "There are sons of the Buddha whose minds are pure," which likewise conveys the sense of pure faith. Furthermore, it is interpreted as referring to the Jewel of the Buddha.
The Teacher is like a guide; the Dharma Jewel is like a guide; the Sangha Jewel is like a good companion; and the precepts are like the mount upon which one rides.

Whether one is a person, a Buddha, or a follower of the Dharma, those who seek the unsurpassed Dharma Jewel must take the World-Honored One as their great guide to lead sentient beings into the correct path of the Dharma.
Furthermore, they must draw near to virtuous friends who have left the household life to serve as companions, practicing and maintaining purity.
The precepts serve as the vehicle to lead one toward the precious destination of Buddhahood. Once that destination is reached, one abandons the causes of poverty and low status;
by revering the Triple Gem, one is able to transcend the evil realms. For this reason, the initial statement "thus" is intended to inspire faith.

Regarding the "realization through faith" (*śraddhābhisamaya*), the ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there are six types of realization, of which the realization through faith is the first.
First: "The four who rely on the excellence of ultimate virtue" refers to the practice of the Path. "Rely" (hé) means to bear or carry. "Ultimate virtue" (zhìdé) refers to the fruit of Buddhahood;
"virtue" (dé) is so called because it denotes the noble. "House" (jiā) signifies goodness. Those who establish faith therein are [those who abide in] the eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

Regarding these virtuous causes, those who wish to realize and enter these four must all possess faith. For one who belongs to the family that partakes of the flavor of the Dharma, it is like this: when one wishes to eat food, one must have hands;
likewise, when one wishes to consume the flavor of the Dharma, it cannot be done without faith. Therefore, it is said that "faith is the hand of the family.
As for the phrase "like a great dragon-elephant," does this mean it is a dragon like an elephant, or that it is an elephant that is a dragon? It is a dragon...

"Elephants and dragons are distinct. Some explain that "dragon-elephants" (nāga-hastin) are two separate things; however, this is not the case here. It is said that the Emperor released various great elephants into the Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇagiri*).
Within those mountains there are dragon palaces, and he commanded the dragons to mate with the elephants so that elephant offspring would be born.

Because they are the progeny of the dragons, they are called "dragon-elephants. These dragon-elephants travel more than ten thousand *li* in a single day. As it is said: [the passage continues as in the source].
The Han Emperor [established] the former horse stations at the edge of the Great Dragon Pond (Dàlóngchí) in Lánzhōu; because colts were born there, they were called "Dragon Horses" (Lóngmǎ).

Thus, the dragon and the elephant are taken as metaphors for those who have entered the Path, who are able to sever afflictions (kleśa) and whose majestic virtue is lofty and far-reaching, just like the dragon and the elephant.
Regarding the phrase "taking faith as the trunk," it means that if an elephant lacked its trunk, its body...
It destroys life at its end. If a person lacks faith, there is no way for them to realize the Path. Regarding "using equanimity as the tusks":
just as an elephant has tusks that can repel enemies, a person who possesses equanimity can extinguish greed and anger; thus, no afflictions whatsoever are able to cause harm.
This is because one takes non-greed and so forth as equanimity. Regarding "using mindfulness as the neck": the elephant has a neck...

Therefore, the neck and head are connected. If a person possesses mindfulness (*smṛti*), maintaining it without forgetting, all wholesome karma (*kuśala-karma*) will continue in succession without interruption.
Regarding "taking wisdom (*prajñā*) as the head": the head is foremost; it discerns the path.
Wisdom stands supreme, distinguishing right from wrong. The Master of Bingzhou said: "The 'head' mentioned here intends to signify the two eyes, which are able to see the road."

Because it is the most intelligent, it is likened to the two wisdoms of the fundamental nature and subsequent attainment, as they are able to skillfully distinguish between the wrong path and the right path.
"Carrying and gathering wholesome dharmas upon its two shoulders" refers to shame and remorse serving as the two shoulders; it is by means of shame and remorse that this is accomplished.
It is able to bear and gather wholesome dharmas, honoring and respecting the virtuous and good while rejecting the violent and evil.
One may also say that since wisdom was previously described as the head, these two—precept and concentration—are the two shoulders.
The "matrix of the five sevenfold noble riches" (*saptavidha-ārya-dhana*) refers to the initial matrix, which is also the beginning. It is like a foundation being the very first thing.
"Beginning and matrix together" is like a child in the womb being called "the beginning. These noble riches serve as the antidote to the three kinds of worldly riches:
first, the riches of increase, which refers to things such as presses, saws, wind-blown hammers, and axes, which are capable of removing [obstructions].

All afflictions increase the skin and flesh; these are also called "wealth. Second is the wealth of delight. Regarding the scholar who is a great merchant of the fundamental rules of the Dharma-treasure:
this refers to one who studies the Dharma, being like a merchant who exchanges merit for wisdom and wisdom for merit, just as in a secular market.
Such a person is called a merchant, serving as a metaphor for those who trade in things such as gold, silver, and fine silks. They are the same.

These precious objects are able to bring about satisfaction; thus, they constitute the three kinds of auspicious wealth (*śrī-dhana*). This refers to the various items such as the hundred cords and ritual implements bestowed during the four seasons and the eight festivals.
Regarding this, people in the West, upon reaching these seasonal occasions, frequently present auspicious *kuśa* grass, fresh flowers, and the like, in order to manifest auspiciousness.
Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are mundane and supramundane forms of wealth.

There are fifteen remedies in total. To summarize them in verse: The six types of conduct and pleasure are not pervasive; Time, place, exhaustion, leading, liberation, Sufficiency, going, suffering, and evil are the opposites;
Calamity, burning, and lack of cessation. First, regarding "conduct": this refers to worldly wealth and treasures.
It increases unwholesome conduct and will inevitably cause one to sink into the cycle of birth and death.

The supramundane noble wealth can give rise to wholesome conduct and enable practitioners to ascend to the further shore. Regarding the two types of happiness: worldly wealth provides pleasure for only a single body;
yet it brings constant sorrow and affliction due to the oppression of kings and officials. Supramundane noble wealth leads inevitably to eternal bliss. Third.

The five worldly desires and material wealth do not penetrate the six sense faculties; they only provide relief for the two realms of form and desire. Because one is addicted to these material riches, they are limited.

In contrast, the supramundane noble wealth penetrates the six sense faculties, extensively covering the three realms of existence and providing relief from the five desires throughout the four modes of birth.
Fourth, regarding worldly wealth: it exists at times and is absent at others; though one may enjoy it throughout a lifetime, it disperses again upon the end of life.
Because the supramundane noble wealth exists at all times even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [it is superior]. Fifth, regarding the levels (*bhūmi*):

worldly wealth—consisting of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—exists only within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). The supramundane noble wealth, however, pervades the nine levels. Sixth, regarding exhaustion: worldly wealth...
Worldly wealth is subject to exhaustion, whereas the supramundane noble wealth is inexhaustible throughout kalpas; this is the sense of the lotus flower emerging from the water being inexhaustible.
For example, it is like one lamp igniting hundreds of thousands of lamps: those in darkness all become bright, and that light never comes to an end. Regarding the seventh "introduction":
worldly wealth can lead one into birth and death, causing one to sink and wallow in the ocean of suffering; the supramundane noble wealth, however, can lead [one to liberation].
Because the practitioner reaches enlightenment. Regarding the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*): worldly wealth belongs to five parties;
kings, thieves, water, fire, and unfilial children share it as their masters. Thus, there is a sense in which it can be lost. Worldly treasures of the supramundane, however, cannot be lost;
they become ever more radiant throughout successive kalpas. Regarding the nine [destinies]: worldly wealth cannot cause a person to go to nirvāṇa; [only] supramundane [wealth can do so].
The noble wealth (ārya-dhana) can lead sentient beings out of birth and death; therefore, it is "sufficient.

As for worldly treasures, even if one possesses a thousand billion, stinginess increases all the more; when bestowed upon others, one never feels satiated. World-transcending treasures, however, are freely bestowed upon the poor;
even if they were to fill the kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, there would be no stinginess, for they cause all sentient beings to have sufficient use of them. Ten.

First, regarding suffering and affliction: even if worldly wealth and treasures were to fill hundreds of thousands of millions, suffering and affliction would be even greater, for one is not independent due to being bound by kings and subject to exile.
The supramundane noble wealth, however, suffices throughout the entire dharma-realm and is free from sorrow and affliction.
Thus, the *Śāstra on Bestowing Liberation* says: "Seeking much brings the suffering of empty matters and the suffering of affliction; having few desires is itself nirvana."
Regarding the twelve antidotes to evil: worldly wealth and treasures must be constantly guarded against theft or loss, which prevents one from sleeping soundly.
However, supramundane wealth is serene and free of obstruction; thus, the *Fuzi* (Treatise on the Son) says: "Excellent, O son of the Śākya!

You may float or sink according to your nature; like a hairpin removed from the profane world, you have cast off sorrow. Herein, it should be explained that this reverses the [notion of] the "son" being high.
[It is said that] they are called the causes and conditions of happiness (and so forth). Regarding the thirteen calamities: worldly wealth and treasures nourish the body of the five desires;

though one hopes for the security of the self, they inevitably become sources of disaster. Thus, that treatise states: "Among the great calamities of the world, none surpass birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The consort recalls the countenance of her peach and plum blossoms, yet the likeness [of her beauty] is pressed by the years of the setting sun. Furthermore, as for the time of initial birth—

At that time, he constantly dwelt in foul and filthy places; his hair was white and his face was wrinkled, such that no one took pleasure in him. He groaned as he sat or rose, with but little life remaining.
One day, when his life ended, his corpse lay prostrate upon the ground, its complexion changed and oozing with filth; yet in his lifetime, he had cherished his son dearly.
One should stay far away and not look at it. Even when one weeps for a brief moment, people know it and laugh; thus, one knows that this body is truly a calamity.
Regarding the fourteenth [point], "burning affliction," that treatise provides an analogy: it is like a person suffering from scabies who approaches a fire to roast themselves.

Because the itching feels pleasant at first, they eventually grab it with their hands, unaware that after a short while the pain will become unbearable. The bodies of sentient beings are likewise addicted to wealth.

They crave forms and colors and compete for fame and profit, like one who, while finding a momentary relief from itching by leaning toward a fire, subsequently falls into the evil realms—how is this different from the pain of scratching a scab?
Fifteenth, regarding non-interruption: worldly wealth and treasures have a limit and will eventually be exhausted;
the supramundane noble treasures, however, can never be exhausted. Thus, the sutra below says: "If one were to use these vehicles and goods to provide for an entire kingdom, it would still—"
It is not yet exhausted; how much less so for the various sons.
The "initial joy" (*chùlè*) of the six virtues and nine causes: "initial" (*chù*) signifies the beginning. Spring is the beginning (*chū*) of the year;

autumn is the beginning of the harvest. Thus, the *Erya* states: "Initial (*chù*), harvest (*luò*), commencement (*quányú*), inception (*zhào*), death (*cú*), origin (*yuánshǐ*), etc., all mean the beginning."
This is the meaning. Question: For what reason are only eight causes enumerated? Explanation: Because desire arises only after one has first developed faith;
faith is the basis for desire, and it is through this that aspiration occurs. Thus, among these eight causes, faith is always the first.
Taking wholesome dharmas as the foundation, one possesses goodness before faith arises; faith is born from goodness. Regarding the nine causes of goodness:

first, the names are listed individually; second, they are assigned to their respective categories; third, based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, each name is stated in a single phrase followed by its explanation, with further detailed commentary for each (as can be seen in the sub-commentary).
As for the statement that "desire serves as the basis for giving rise to aspiration," "hope" (*āśā*) means longing.
"Recollection" (*smṛti*) and "expectation" (*āśā*) refer to seeking and longing; therefore, they are called "desire" (*chanda*). Furthermore, desire has three meanings:
first, wholesome desire; second, unwholesome desire; and third, indeterminate desire. Regarding the first, wholesome desire, there are four types of wholesomeness:

first, mundane wholesomeness, which refers to giving rise to vows and aspirations that seek only the fruits and retributions of the mundane triple world. Within this mundane desire, it is said that one first seeks the desire realm.
First, the pursuit of the wondrous objects of the five sensory realms, such as form and so forth;

second, the pursuit of the form realm, which consists of the fruits of the four dhyānas and the sprinkling of one’s body with the nectar of joy and bliss after having transcended them; third, the pursuit of the formless realm, such as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Second, the desire of the śrāvaka, which is the longing for the Four Noble Truths; third, the desire of the pratyekabuddha, which is the seeking of dependent origination for the sake of one’s own benefit and happiness.
The four types of bodhisattva desire consist in practicing the six *pāramitās* for the sake of benefiting oneself and others.
However, worldly desires result in the extreme suffering of the three miserable realms; even though they are virtuous, when compared to the Three Vehicles, they are still considered suffering.

What is here called "desire as the root" refers specifically to the aspiration for unsurpassed *bodhi*. As for those of the Two Vehicles, who sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and aspire...

Those who have realized *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* are Bodhisattvas; they sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and aspire to realize *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*, which is why it is called "aspiration.
Second, unwholesome aspiration refers to delighting in killing, stealing, and the ten non-virtuous actions, as well as the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*).

Since it has already been stated that these are the fruits of sinking into the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), the "three types of desire for the indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) refer to the cultivation of deportment (*īryāpatha*), craftsmanship (*śilpa*), and calligraphy/painting.
Regarding the second, "attention" (*manasikāra*): according to the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, its intrinsic nature is one of the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Since this constitutes a form of desire from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, one must still arouse the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*) to seek and attain Bodhi. There is no [other way].

Because of weariness [with cyclic existence]. Regarding that which arises from the gathering of the three contacts: in the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, contact is established as the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Since this is what is required, one applies diligent attention (*manasikāra*), neither wishing for the arising of unwholesome or indeterminate states of mind in the world, but seeking only the fruit of sublime Bodhi.
This is because one takes Bodhi itself as the essential nature and object of focus (*ālambana*). It is like a worker in the West who focuses his mind with single-mindedness.
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times; once these ten recitations are accomplished, one will attain birth in the Western Land.

One should then direct the mind-king toward that West, for the West is the supreme and sublime object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Regarding the phrase "the four types of feeling (*vedanā*) are induced and subsumed within the mind":

this is like when, having heard a lecture on superior teachings, one gives rise to the aspiration to study them; one must necessarily apply focused attention (*manasikāra*) to receive and internalize them.

One must collect the mind and maintain it. If, among the three types of wisdom—those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—one listens but does not receive [the teachings], how is this different from pouring clear water into an overturned basin?
It is laborious yet without benefit. As for the five concentrations being the "predominant mind," it is because they are subtly tranquil.

If one wishes to give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*), one must first attain meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If the mind is not settled and merely pursues external objects, it will be distracted and unstable;
how then can wisdom arise? Therefore, it is said that concentration can bring forth wisdom, for wisdom is born from concentration.

For those of the Hīnayāna, this involves practices such as the contemplations on white bones, water and fire, forests, impurity, and the analysis of the non-self and the elements (*dhātu*). As for Bodhisattvas, however—

One practices the contemplations of Consciousness-Only, Signlessness, Non-arising, True Suchness, and the Three Natures. Having entered these contemplations, the mind and intellect become pure, and one finds joy therein.
Thus a poem says: "Entering meditative absorption, one contemplates emptiness and existence; emerging from absorption, one chants of emptiness and existence.
As one departs from and enters absorption, one again contemplates the mind of emptiness and existence. A verse states: "The Bodhisattva’s cool moon is like ultimate emptiness."
When the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within it. It is like a vast marsh or a long river where the blue waves extend for ten thousand *qǐng*;
the clear sky scatters its radiance, mirroring the clouds and heavens. The meditative mind of sentient beings is also like this:
it must be pure and bright, far removed from discursive攀緣 (*pānyuán*). Then the clouds and heavens of wisdom will reflect the radiant colors of Bodhi—brilliant, crystal clear, and luminously serene.
Be careful. Thus, a poem says: "The waters are vast and the fragrance remains distant; the river is long and the cloud-shadows are deep. Therefore, one must cultivate concentration (*samādhi*).

Regarding the statement that the sixth wisdom is the most excellent because it discriminates between good and evil: since wisdom arises by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one must distinguish between right and wrong, and between the heterodox and the orthodox.
If one lacks wisdom, one will inevitably sink into the teachings of external paths and false views. Since one is already able...
Discernment consists solely in aspiring for perfect enlightenment; this is the most supreme and wondrous. As the analogy goes:

when the Dharma Master of Puzhou was lecturing, there were many people at first, but later there was only a single woman. The Dharma Master asked, "For what reason do you not go to other places to listen?
She replied, "When your disciple sees a large assembly of monks, it means the lecture is excellent. Your disciple only desires a sincere heart, yet she does not understand the Dharma Master."
Regarding the language: The Dharma Master sighed and said, "This woman is one who understands the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Why?

Because wisdom (*prajñā*) is capable of discerning that which is most excellent. As for 'the seven liberations being firm so as to cease the fetters,' since she is able to unify concentration and wisdom, the two obstacles must both be eliminated.
Because both afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions have been abandoned, she is called 'liberated' (*vimukti*)."
It is firm and no longer subject to further defilement, for it has brought the fetters to rest. Regarding the phrase "the eighth is the final limit because the path of awakening is fulfilled":
having emerged from the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one then aspires to seek the single, wondrous *dharmakāya* nirvāṇa;
therefore, it is said that the path of awakening is fulfilled. The "final body" (*paścima-deha*) is precisely the *dharmakāya*. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The body of the Tathāgata..."
This refers to the final body, the body free from nutriment; such is its meaning. From what do these eight kinds of factors emerge?
They emerge through liberation. Through what does liberation arise? It arises through wisdom. And so on, until: for what purpose is desire?
It is solely by means of faith; thus the commentary states: "Since faith is the basis for desire, it is made to arise first. The present statement, "in this manner," is intended to engender faith.
Alternatively, "the faculty" (*ki*) is like a door pivot (*kaku*); hence the *Shuji* says: "Once the pivot and the mechanism are set in motion..."
The ultimate points of honor and disgrace are also the beginning.
"Seven" refers to the opening of the gate of the mechanism; "opening" means to assemble or to initiate. "Mechanism" (ji) refers to the mechanism of what is produced.
It refers to those sentient beings who are submerged in the five sufferings, mired in the mud. The Tathāgata gives rise to great kindness and great compassion, extensively expounding the teachings.
First, he clarifies the introductory section (*nidāna*) to inspire faith in the Tathāgata; he first causes sentient beings to take faith as their hand.

Subsequently, he expounds the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*), wherein the three [vehicles] are unified into one. This is like the teaching-hand reaching downward to meet the sentient beings, for which they must then employ the hand of faith.

"Upward. Joining both hands signifies the ability to extract one from suffering. It is precisely this meaning that refers to the extinction of all kinds of darkness and the extraction of sentient beings from the mire of birth and death.

That which covers sentient beings and gives rise to the hindrances of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), obstructing them from *nirvāṇa* and causing them to sink into the flow of desire, is called the hindrance of affliction.
Furthermore, because delusion and ignorance (*avidyā*) obstruct wisdom, it is called [the hindrance of cognitive obstructions].

Regarding the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): Now, when the Tathāgata teaches the various doctrines to cause sentient beings to sever the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realize Great Nirvāṇa, this is called the "virtue of abandonment" (*prahāṇaguṇa*).
Furthermore, causing wisdom to increase day by day and removing the cognitive obstacles is called the "virtue of knowledge" (*jñānaguṇa*).
Moreover, pulling sentient beings out of the mud is the "virtue of grace" (*anugrahaguṇa*). Here, what is termed "mud" refers to the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The earth represents the afflictions and ignorance, which have been intermingled since beginningless time; hence it is called "mud.
Alternatively, karma is taken as the water, for it can summon an indeterminate body and cause all sentient beings to pass from birth into death;
thus it is termed "mud. Furthermore, faith is like a hand: it is like boarding a great ship and sailing upon the vast ocean; if one lacks hands, one will drift and sink.
The masses of living beings are like waves; if there were hands to move and grasp them, not one would sink. Thus we know that if a person lacks two hands, how can they board a boat?
If a person lacks faith, how can they cultivate the Way? Therefore, it is established thus: first, one must give rise to faith.
Now, this mind of faith is one of the twenty-one mental factors (*caitasika*) within the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*. If such [faith] exists...
Faith. Furthermore, when encountering favorable conditions, the twenty-one dharmas increase in every moment of thought.

However, if one encounters adverse conditions and gives rise to lack of faith, these twenty-one dharmas, moment by moment, turn toward the unwholesome. Thus, one does not cease drifting and falls into the mire.
Therefore, the *Utpatti-sarga-sūtra* states that King Yama spoke this verse to the sinners: "You have obtained a human body..."
To cultivate goodness is like returning empty-handed from a mountain of treasures. What you have created now, you yourself shall receive;
what can your wailing avail you now? (and so forth).
The eighth is the clear pearl that purifies the water of the tranquil mind. Because one possesses faith, the mind is immediately pure; if one lacks faith, its nature becomes turbid and yellow.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Faith is like the water-clearing pearl, which can purify turbid water.
When people in the West wish to clarify the turbid water of a pond, they take a bamboo pole, tie a thread to its tip, and attach that bright pearl to it.
Tie a thread to its head and further place a fine wheel upon it; beneath the wheel is a pearl. Place this in turbid water, and the water in the entire pond becomes pure at once.
To apply the analogy: the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, is like the bamboo pole; his preaching of the Dharma is like the thread; and the bright moon gem is like faith.
If sentient beings hear even a single four-line verse of the World-Honored One’s preaching of the Dharma...
By means of these verses, one gives rise to pure faith; moment by moment, it eliminates the turbid waters of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
Therefore, it is said that faith is like a clear pearl. One should recite the "Verses on the Cool Moon of the Bodhisattva" as a record of this.
The ninth section, "Establishing Renown as a Fine Resource for the Way," explains that "renown" (*ming*) refers to fame, while "the Way" (*dao*) refers to the Way of virtue.

Regarding renown, it is said: "When there was no name, heaven and earth began; when there was a name, it became the mother of all things. Furthermore, this name is not a fixed name. As for the Way, it is said:

"The Way that can be spoken of is not the eternal Way. "Fine" (*liang*) means good or excellent. "Resource" (*zi*) means that which flows and circulates. Thus, the gentleman establishes his person and practices the Way.

Goodness, benevolence, righteousness, wisdom, and trustworthiness constitute what is called the Way and its Virtue. Confucius said: "The former kings possessed the ultimate virtue and essential Way by which they brought harmony to the world;
these were precisely benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom, and trustworthiness. Now, when we speak of the names of the Way, they refer to ritual and righteousness.
Thus, we know that a ruler relies on trustworthiness, a minister on loyalty, a father on compassion, and a son on filial piety.
Insects rely on their wings; fish rely on their tails; birds rely on their eggs; and beasts rely on their milk—these are the means by which they are taught to sustain their lives.
Zuǒ Qiūmíng said: "The three things—military force, food, and good faith—must not be abandoned. Yet, if a state has no military force, it has no means to crush its enemies.

If a state has no food, the common people will suffer from famine and desolation; when the foundation is not secure, how can the nation be at peace? Furthermore, as for good faith, if a state lacks it..."
[The ruler] stands [alone]. The way of sovereign and subject is not practiced; there is no trust between sovereign and subject, and calamity and disorder break out.
Thus we know that trust is the hallmark of a gentleman’s state. If there is trust, one knows that a state exists.
The *Lüshi Chunqiu* says: "The merit of verbal trust is great indeed. If Heaven acts without trust, it cannot complete the year. If Earth acts without trust, then..."
Plants and trees do not grow large. When they encounter the spring wind, if the wind is not sincere, their flowers will not bloom.

When they encounter the summer heat, if the heat is not sincere, the myriad things will not flourish. When they encounter the autumn rain, if the rain is not sincere, their grain will not ripen firmly.

In winter, cold is attained. If this cold were not real, then the earth would not be firm. Thus we know that even with the vastness of heaven and earth and the transformations of the four seasons, they are established through the interplay of the real and the unreal; how much less could such things be achieved by incantations?

"Ten Points on the Excellence of Sincere Hospitality. *Kuan* (欵) means "bent," "different," or "intimate. *Zhongcheng* (衷誠) means "sincerity" or "faithfulness. *Jia* (佳) means "excellent" or "good. *Dai* (待) means "hospitality" or "ritual treatment.
*Zun* (尊) means "honorable" or "superior. Furthermore, there is clear sincerity. *Zhaozhi* (沼沚) refers to small pools of water. *Mao* (毛) refers to the "produce of the soil.
This includes grasses, *feicui* (翡翠—likely referring to specific plants or fibers), *mao-mao* (貓毛—cat hair), ox tails, rabbit fur, and so forth. *Ping* (蘋) [refers to the plant *Blyxa octandra*].
The "great duckweed" (*bǔ*) is the *píng*. The *fán* is called *póqí* in the *Chūnqiū*; *póqí* is the same as *póhē*. The *yùnzǎo* is sea-weed (*hǎizǎo*).
"Fit for offering" (*kějiàn*) means to present as a tribute; "delicacy" (*xiū*) means that which is superior. One might ask: how can these coarse plants be considered rare or extraordinary?
Yet, when one approaches the sea and encounters them, they appear strange. The intention is to clarify that all of them possess their own regularity and reliability. And...
Moreover, as for a gentleman establishing the trust between two states: the two states of Qi and Lu were constantly at war with one another.

When the state of Lu sought peace, Qi said, "Only when you bring the cauldron (ding) shall I grant you peace. The state of Lu presented the cauldron, yet Qi was still unwilling to accept it, fearing that it might be demanded again.
They invited a person of integrity—also named Ji Zha—to deliver it; only then did I [Qi] agree to accept it. Had it not been for this...
"I shall certainly not accept it, for I fear it may be a forgery. Ji-zhan was a Great Officer of Lu. Regarding the statement that "the great carriage has no *ni*":
in a four-horse carriage, a dragon's head and body are fixed to the shafts and secured by a transverse wooden bar; when a single horse pulls it, it moves. This is called the *ni*.
To say that the carriage lacks the *ni* refers to the curved portion at the tip of the shaft where it rests upon the neck of the ox.

It is made of wood. When it is bound with ropes at its joints, it becomes a *ni* (yoke-head). Furthermore, according to the *Chunqiu jie* (Exegesis on the Spring and Autumn Annals), there is an account regarding the mutual trust between two states:
Qin and Wei were in discord and constantly waged war against one another. Later, when Wei sought peace, Qin demanded of Wei:

"If you obtain the Three-legged Precious Tripod, send it to our country; we shall then grant peace. Wei was reluctant to part with the precious tripod, so they instead sent a different vessel that leaked water.
The cauldron was sent to the state of Qin. The ruler of Qin replied, saying: "If you send it with Liu Xiahui and Wei Bu, I will accept it;
however, if the Lord of Wei comes in person, I shall not accept it. This is because those two men possess benevolence and integrity, and would not act recklessly toward me.
The Lord of Wei then commanded Liu Xiahui and Ji Xi-qing to take this cauldron [to him].
The reward was granted to the Lord of Qin. Ji Xi spoke in the Qin dialect: "Your servant cannot leave; this tripod is indeed a forgery and cannot be used to repay the State of Qin.
The State of Wei is the true possessor of the tripod. The Lord of Wei was greatly incensed. Ji Xi submitted a memorial, saying:

"The one who is trustworthy is the servant’s state; the tripod belongs to Your Majesty’s state. How could Your Majesty take a forged tripod and cause your servant to lose his integrity? Your servant would rather die."

The person cannot fail to maintain their word. When the Wei ruler found his words difficult to accept, [the Master] said: "If you do not trust a state with its myriad chariots, yet you trust the two words of these two sons, it is entirely because of 'trust' (xin).
This is like the Duke of Yanling’s trust, which arose from hanging his sword upon a pine branch; and like the matter in the *Sūtra* of the Dharma Master Wangming.
If one follows the *Sūtra*, it accords with taking the first instance from the *Spring and Autumn Annals*: the exchange of hostages between Zhou and Zheng. This precisely accords with the *Sūtra*.
One should examine this with care. Furthermore, there are two aspects to the meaning of faith (*śraddhā*).

Just as one crossing the vast ocean relies on hands to steer the boat, so too does one crossing the river of birth and death rely on the practice of faith to give rise to wisdom (that is, to transcend birth and death). It is like traveling through a desolate wilderness while possessing hands, holding armor and a staff to ward off enemies;
so it is that one who emerges from birth and death possesses faith. Through faith, wisdom is generated and afflictions are severed (that is, one is able to...).
[This leads to] the arousal of wisdom and understanding).

Furthermore, regarding the preceding ten gates, which rely on the understanding of the ultimate and conventional truths, they must arise only when the mind possesses purity and the intention of faith is aroused.
If the water of the mind is turbid, there will be no intention of faith. It is not yet known which passage within the three cycles of this sutra clarifies this point.

"Purity of faith and sincerity. The commentary explains: The first cycle of the subsequent sutra states that the Buddhas appear in the five turbidities of a degenerate age—namely, the turbidity of the eon, and so forth, up to the turbidity of life.
Sentient beings have heavy defilements, being stingy, greedy, and jealous.

It is by accomplishing the Buddhas through skillful means that, within the single Buddha-vehicle, they distinguish and teach the existence of three vehicles. This is precisely because of the turbidity of their minds and their lack of faith in the one [vehicle]. In the one...

This is divided into three parts. Since it has now been taught as one, it is pure. As the subsequent sutra says: "Possessing a sense of shame and remorse," up to the extensive praise of the One Vehicle path;
and again, "The mind of the Buddha-son is pure," and so forth. Thus, we know that the purity of mind is precisely the mind of faith (*śraddhā*).
Because this mind of faith has emerged, the One Vehicle is taught. In the second week [of the teaching], it says: "O Śāriputra, you have already attained [realization] through faith in this sutra..."

[They] enter. This continues until [the point where it is] no longer within the scope of their own wisdom. Furthermore, it says: "If a person has faith and takes refuge in the Buddha," and so forth. In the third cycle [of teachings], it states:
"O Bhikṣus, when the Tathāgata himself knows that the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived, and that the assembly possesses purity," and so on.

Therefore, if one wishes to enter the wisdom of relinquishment of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), one must necessarily possess faith. Thus, it was previously stated that faith is the primary faculty for entering the Dharma.

This is precisely its meaning. Question: Why is it necessary to resolve the mind (*cittotpāda*) and give rise to a mind of faith? Explanation: There are four types. First, resolving the mind upon seeing the Dharma about to perish.
Second, resolving the mind upon seeing sentient beings suffering due to evil karma. Third, resolving the mind upon seeing the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Fourth, resolving the mind by reading and reciting the Mahāyāna and contemplating its principles with discernment. It is through these four meanings that one subsequently gives rise to the mind of faith.
Regarding the explanation of the text as revolving according to four meanings, it may be understood as follows. "Revolve" (pravartate) means to arise or to emerge.

Although four meanings are mentioned, if one examines them closely, there are actually seven. First, regarding the section on "revolving by way of analogy," this uses the present to illustrate the past;
or, as in the phrase "as for what has already been explained," this uses the present to compare with the ancient. Within the second [meaning], there are also two sentences; the first...
Regarding the instructions on the teachings concerning the near and the distant: the section beginning with "or" (*vā*) constitutes the instruction itself.
The third [turn] consists of a single [type], namely the turn of question and answer. The fourth also has two [types]: the first is the turn of granting permission;

the second, from "or" (*vā*) onwards, is the turn of conviction. These together form seven sentences. The Dharma Master of Bingzhou said: "This [fourth turn] has three [sub-types]: first, the turn based on analogy."
Second, the transformation based on skillful means; third, the transformation by comparing the present with the past. Regarding the first, the transformation through analogy:
as it is said, "Such is the wealth and nobility of Sudatta that he resembles Vaiśravaṇa of the north.

Because the Northern Heavenly King possesses the most supreme merit, he is singled out for mention. Or, as in the case of a hall where the central western pillar is round and straight, no different from the eastern pillar.
This is a simile. Alternatively, it may be understood thus: this person’s brilliant discernment is like that bright sun, capable of dispelling darkness and gloom;
there is no difference whatsoever. All these are turned as similes. As for their application to the Dharma, Ānanda said:
"Thus [it is] spoken today, just as the Tathāgata spoke in the past; there is no difference whatsoever. Therefore, he says "thus" (*evam*). Second.
Regarding the transformation through skillful means, it is as has been traditionally taught. Third, regarding the transformation by using the present to illustrate the past:
that which the Tathāgata spoke in the past was the teaching of the fundamental substance (*mūla-dharma*).

What I now speak—these sūtra passages and verses—likewise causes one to abandon the provisional and grasp the real, to practice the cause of the One Vehicle, and to realize the fruit of the One Vehicle; just as I heard it in the past, there is no difference whatsoever.
This is the teaching of the reflected image. Although I cannot personally realize it, these textual expressions of the reflected image that I have spoken are exactly as I heard them in the past;
they are certainly not different. Alternatively, these textual expressions may have been transmitted by Ānanda.
The original substance teaching is that which sentient beings hear and receive for the purpose of practice.

The reflected image teaching refers to others besides these two. Regarding Ānanda alone: in relation to the Buddha, he is a reflection; however, in relation to sentient beings, he is the original substance.

That which is neither the original substance nor a reflection refers to Ānanda in relation to sentient beings: because he transmits the teachings, he is not the original substance; yet because he did not hear them directly from the Buddha, he is not a reflection.
As for what has been explained: furthermore, it is not a reflection; the rest may be understood. Regarding the progression of the question and answer, it may be understood from the commentary.
This present question and answer is as follows: "You are going to the temple," to which he replies, "Ā, I have already gone. He says "Ā" (pronounced *ǝ* with the initial *ǝ* reversed).
According to common vernacular usage, one should simply say "ruò" (pronounced *jwo* with the initial *jwo* reversed). "Ruò" means "if"; "ruò" also means "like" (*yǐ*). It is just like this.
Such are these and other similar expressions. Regarding "turning according to permission," it may be understood from the commentary.
According to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there is also the turning according to permission. Subhūti asked: "How should one dwell? How should one subdue the mind?
The Buddha replied: "One should dwell thus... up to "...its mind. At the beginning, he first granted permission, and only thereafter [proceeded].
He extensively expounded the meaning of subduing [the afflictions] and abiding in the Path, and also permitted [others] to turn the wheel [of Dharma].
Furthermore, among Ānanda’s converted disciples, he was foremost in *dhāraṇī*; in receiving the Buddha’s words, he was like a vessel pouring water into a basin, without any omission.
Therefore, that we are able today to transmit the teachings of the Dharma without differing from the Buddha is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:

"Though vessels made of diamond, copper, iron, or precious gems differ, when they are filled with water, there is no difference in the taste of the water. One cannot claim the taste of the water differs because of the distinctness of the vessels;
nor can one claim the vessels are identical because the taste of the water does not differ. Such is the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma and its transmission.
"Ānanda, Ānanda received it and transmitted it to the great Bodhisattvas and the great Śrāvakas. The Bodhisattvas and others, in turn, transmitted it to us.

Although the individuals who transmitted it differ, the essence of the teaching is one and the same; one must not claim that because the transmitters are distinct, there is any discrepancy in the teaching."
One cannot claim that because the teaching is not different, the capacity of the audience (*indriya*) must be one; this can be understood through appropriate analogies.

Regarding the masters of the commentaries who take the Venerable Paramārtha’s explanation of the three matters of the *saṃgīti* (council) as an interpretation of the term "evam" (*thus*), this is somewhat inappropriate.

If one intends to derive the underlying meaning from "evam," then citing this [explanation] is acceptable; however, if one takes it as an explanation of the semantic meaning of "evam," it is incorrect. (In this context, the origins of the *saṃgīti* should be recounted, as described in other notes.)
"Such is the beginning of resonance and response. These are the words of Liu Qiu, a recluse of Mount Wudu, who annotated the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The Dharma Master of Bingzhou spoke of this analogy: "What is it like when one speaks of resonance and response?
It is like a species of wasp that drills a hole into the nest within the earth, and then takes green grass from amidst the weeds [to line it]."
A worm and a spider were within their burrow. Every day, he recited this mantra: "Like me! Like me!
After many days had passed in this manner, two horns grew upon the head of the worm. After further time had elapsed, six legs grew from beneath its belly;
its waist was slender, no different from that of a bee, and its wings fully developed like those of a large bee, so that it could fly upward.

They are different. To apply this through analogy: the insect is the stimulus (*gan*), and the bee is the response (*ying*). The harmony between stimulus and response is no different from that of the bee.
The manifested births of all Buddhas are likewise thus. When sentient beings provide the stimulus, the Tathāgata immediately responds by preaching the wondrous Dharma to lead them into the Path.
It is like bringing an insect and placing it within its own nest; once their faculties (*indriya*) have matured, [he acts for them].

The words of the prophecy state: "You sentient beings, from after my parinirvāṇa until the present, if you can give rise to even a single thought of sympathetic joy toward the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, I shall bestow upon you all the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This is the mantra: 'Like me, like me. Having received this prophecy, they immediately realize the Way through both the fundamental essence (*mūla-dharmatā*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)."
Wisdom arises simultaneously [with it], like the two horns growing from the head of that insect. It is able to practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), like the six legs of the insect.

With its supernormal powers (abhijñā) acting with mastery, it travels throughout the ten directions and listens to the True Dharma in the presence of all Buddhas, like that insect or bee flying and soaring with ease.
Therefore, it is said that such things are auspicious omens of responsive resonance. Regarding the phrase "making a track by calling," this refers to the Sūtra.
The first two characters, "rú-shì" (如是), are capable of invoking everything elucidated within this entire scripture:
the provisional and the real, principle and phenomena, the conventional, existence, emptiness, nature, and characteristics—all are thus. The initial term "chè" (轍) refers to a carriage track;
it exhausts the tracks across the earth, just as the two characters "Yōng-zhōu" (雍州) are capable of invoking all [of that region].
There are no common people who do not exhaust [their potential].
That the Venerable Chang-er (Long-ear) Tripiṭaka explains such matters by means of the Three Jewels is an excellent grasp of the meaning of the sūtra. Therefore, the Treatise says:

"The Three Jewels are the most auspicious; therefore, they are spoken of at the beginning of my sūtras. Now, taking the Buddha Jewel as an example, it is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have collectively taught.

Regarding "the synonyms such as 'tathatā' (thusness)" and so forth: the sutra itself states below, "The manner in which the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time preach the Dharma—now I likewise preach the non-discriminative Dharma.
It further states, "From long ago until now, it has been preached thus. Second, regarding the Jewel of the Dharma:
because the characteristics of the Dharma Jewel have not changed from ancient times to the present, they are called "tathatā" and so forth. As stated below: "That is to say..."
All phenomena (*dharmas*) have such characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and such nature (*svabhāva*); their fruits and retributions are equal from beginning to end.

This is what is meant by "suchness" (*tathatā*) as explained in terms of phenomena. Furthermore, it is said that when one is able to know the meaning of such nature and characteristics, then throughout past and present they do not differ;
this is termed "such" (*tatha*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "True" (*zhen*) refers to reality (*bhūta*), and "such" (*ru*) refers to being constant (*nitya*). It is also...
This is the principle that remains unchanged throughout past and present. Regarding the three instances of "Sangha-ratna," it may be understood as explained in the commentary.

Furthermore, it is said: when two things resemble each other, it is called "like" (ru); when there is nothing other than a single thing, it is called "is" (shi). To say that this left hand is exactly like the right hand is termed "like.
This is like the term *yathā* (as it is), where the meaning is "as it is. Since there is no other object, it is termed "is. That is to say:
The treasury of all dharmas spoken by the Buddha is no different from that of the Buddhas of the past; what Ānanda has transmitted is likewise no different.
To call it "thus" (evam) means it is as it was. Since Ānanda heard it directly from the Buddha, it is certainly what Śākyamuni spoke;
to call it "this" (iti) means it is so. Therefore, it is said: "Thus" (evam).
What has been explained above consists, in total, of fifteen interpretations: first, the reason for establishing [the doctrine]; second, one interpretation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*;
third, four interpretations from the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*; fourth, one interpretation by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha;

one interpretation in the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; one in the commentary on the *Anantamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī*; one by Master Zheng Gong; one by Guangzhai; one by Emperor Wu of Liang; and one by Chang... [text ends].
Regarding the three interpretations of the "Thus" (evam) found in the *Śruti-tripiṭaka*, in order to explain these words, a separate commentary on the Tripiṭaka has been set forth.

First, concerning the interpretation as the transmission of the teaching and its meaning: to respectfully accord with the principle is called "Thus" (yathā); to practice in accordance with the teaching is called "Is" (evam). Therefore, it is said "Thus" (evam).
