The stage of 'previously non-existent, now existent' is called arising (*jāti*); the stage of arising that remains for a moment is [called duration...]"* *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full passage continues with the other three characteristics: duration, change, and cessation.)*

It is said that they "abide. Since their abiding differs before and after, another name is established for them. That which exists momentarily and then ceases is called "destruction" (*nirodha*) at the time it is non-existent.

Because the former three exist, they are all situated in the present; because the latter one is non-existent, it is established as the past. How can a non-existent dharma manifest a [characteristic] of existence?

Furthermore, what fault is there in this being a characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Arising (*jāti*) manifests that an existent dharma previously did not exist; destruction (*nirodha*) manifests that an existent...
The non-existence of a phenomenon after its occurrence indicates that this phenomenon is not eternal; its abiding indicates that this phenomenon temporarily possesses utility.

Therefore, although these four characteristics are all termed "indications" (*vijñapti*) with respect to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), their indications differ. These four characteristics are conventionally established based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*);

they may also be conventionally established according to the stages of a single lifetime. The initial existence is called "arising" (*jāti*), and the subsequent non-existence is called "cessation" (*nirodha*). Once arisen...
The continuity of similar [moments] is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Furthermore, this very continuity undergoes change;
therefore, all four characteristics are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*). This explains the moment of a *kṣaṇa*.
From this point onward, the passage clarifies the duration [of time]. The commentary states: "It varies in length according to the limits of one's mental state.

If the body and mind encounter suffering, or if there is indolence, weariness, or delusion, it should be considered long; whereas at times of experiencing pleasure, or during moments of diligent joy and awakening, it is short.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "In a dream, one may think a hundred years have passed, yet upon waking, it is but a brief moment."

Although there is no [time] at the moment of awakening, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa. Furthermore, it is said: "The fool practices for a short time, yet his mind of indolence suspects that it has been long;
the wise one practices for immeasurable kalpas, yet through diligence and vigor, he regards it as a mere moment. This means that because of negligence, the time is long;
because of diligence, the time is short. This principle is clear. Thus, when a man of virtue seeks the methods of the immortals, he passes twelve years with a diligent and striving mind.
He sought the Way of the Immortals. There was an immortal who constantly stayed by his side, reciting incantations and providing instruction.
He established a ritual altar; the immortal, foreknowing what was to come, subsequently dug a pool within the altar grounds. Twelve years later, the period was complete.
"Only one night remains. He said to the valiant man, "Now you must exert yourself; until daybreak, you must not sleep and must not speak.

If you make a sound, you shall not attain the Way of the Immortals, and the celestial deities will slay you. Thereupon, this man concentrated his mind on meditation and refrained from making any noise.
After the immortal had chanted the incantations for a long time, he briefly lost his vigilance and fell asleep. This valiant [man...]
The man then immediately woke from his sleep in an instant and let out a great cry. Thereupon, the deva became enraged and sent fire down from the sky, intending to burn the man.
The rishi dragged him away and immersed him in this pond; only then did he regain consciousness.
Regarding his speech: after twelve years had passed and his practice was successfully accomplished, he suddenly cried out for a short while, unable to maintain his concentration.
The knight replied, "This is karma; it is not my original intention. I merely lost sleep for a moment."
In a dream, I saw myself passing away and being reborn in South India. After I had grown up, I took a wife and fathered a son.
Because a seer had commanded me not to speak, I reached the age of eighty without ever uttering a word. I gave birth to one son whom I cherished with extraordinary affection.
My wife said to me, "If you speak, I will remain here; if you do not speak, I shall take a knife and cut this child."
The child thought it was two segments, yet I remained silent. The wife then killed the child; [the man] raised his blade to kill the child and cried out, but it was not his original intention.
Thus we know that what appeared for a brief moment in a dream has actually passed eighty-odd years.

All this is merely a transformation produced by consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). Those who listen to the Dharma perceive its duration as long or short according to the limitations of their own minds, just as in the following example.
The meaning is that sixty minor kalpas [of the *vyañjana*] are equivalent to the duration of a meal and so forth.
The sub-commentary (*śāstra*) states: "It is not the time of a single arising and ceasing" means it is not the single moment of arising and ceasing within each successive thought-instant (*kṣaṇa*).
It refers exclusively to the five aggregates and all phenomena of both the speaker and the listener, which arise and perish moment by moment.

Once the act of preaching and listening to the Dharma is completed, the three periods of time are provisionally established based on the states of matter (rūpa) and mind (citta), and these are collectively termed "one time. Furthermore, according to the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) of the Liang dynasty, there are three meanings:
first, the time of turning the wheel of Dharma; when the speaker is correctly preaching and the listener is correctly listening, it is called the time of turning the wheel of Dharma.

The second is the time of harmony (*saṃnipāta-kāla*), which refers to the teaching according to the capacity [of the disciples]. It is called the time of harmony because the teacher is appropriately responsive and the response and the stimulus are in accord.
The third is the time of equanimity (*samatā-kāla*), which means hearing the sūtras without falling into dullness or agitation and without error;

this is the initial turning of the wheel of Dharma and is called the time of the phase of "having teachings. Regarding the second, the time of the teaching of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kāla*): the *Lotus Sūtra* is not [merely] empty.
The meaning of "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is subsumed within the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the monastic precepts established by the Buddha:

those who have not received the ordination do not participate in the *poṣadha*. All such precepts must not be recited; they may be heard by kings and ministers, but commoners are not permitted to hear them.
As for the term "time of *samaya*," this is translated as "the time for destroying false views," referring to the five sections of the *Āgamas* and the nine... [text fragment].
The Dharma was distributed without distinction between the "black" and the "white," so that all were able to hear it. Question: At what time was this sutra preached? Answer:
According to the three [turnings], these are times of the distinct characteristics of the Wheel of Dharma; if one refers to the two vehicles, they are also called times for destroying false views.

Therefore, Zhu Fahu translated it as the *Zhengfahua jing* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra). Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) that "those who destroy the heterodox" refers to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), this [text] says "destroying the heterodox" refers to those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Since those of the Two Vehicles are not included among the non-Buddhists, why are they called "heterodox"?
The answer is: as in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, when observing the characteristics of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is said that they practice a heterodox path.

□ Seeing the various Buddhas: from the perspective of the Dharma-body, the Transformation-buddha is provisional (or "false"). From the perspective of the Two Vehicles, the Lesser Vehicle is provisional. What does this mean?
Furthermore, regarding the time of worldly convention, it is as when one says, "At one time, on the bank of the Ganges," and so forth.
Regarding the six dharmas in relation to their objects: according to the Great [Treatise], at this time, the essence is solely...

The sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its objects the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which it cannot otherwise discern. When these [other consciousnesses] are unable to function as objects, the seventh consciousness (*manas*) likewise clings to the eighth as the self;
however, it only takes internal objects and cannot take external ones. Therefore, it is only at such times that the sixth consciousness can take them as objects.
Nevertheless, this is explained from the perspective of those who lack mastery. If one speaks from the perspective of those who possess mastery—such as the Tathāgatas—[the situation is different].
The eight consciousnesses each take time-periods (*adhvan*) as their objects. If categorized according to *dharmas*, they are subsumed solely within the *dharmadhātu* and the *dharmāyatana*.

If categorized according to objective spheres (*viṣaya*), they are subsumed generally within the *viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*. In the Sarvāstivāda school, there is no substantial entity of time among the fourteen *viprayuktas*;

rather, the substance of time is distinguished upon the basis of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). This is a case of subsuming the provisional under the real. Within this context, it should be [understood] as fourfold.

Analysis of the Categories: First, subsuming the provisional under the real. This refers to the Sarvāstivāda school, which establishes the temporal divisions based solely on the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

This differs from the Mahāyāna, which posits these as provisional designations upon the various states of matter and mind (*rūpa-citta*). Since this school maintains that all phenomena possess substantial reality, it is said to "subsume the provisional under the real.
Second, subsuming the real under the provisional. This refers to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which [establishes time] solely by means of the three... [text fragment ends].

Regarding "number": the mind of consciousness (*vijñāna*) conceptually discriminates the provisional characteristics of worldly numbers because it perceives them as manifest characteristics upon consciousness.

From the perspective of the correct doctrine of the Mahāyāna, this is also the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), and it is also substantially existent. Among the three types of perfuming, this is the perfuming of names and conventions (*nāma-vyañjana-vāsanā*).
That which is both real and provisional refers precisely to the correct doctrine of the Mahāyāna: while the substance of consciousness is real, its various states (*avasthā*) are provisional.
The designation "time" (kāla) is conventionally established; its essence consists of the fourteen non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) categorized as temporal units.
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), it is subsumed under the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it is subsumed under the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Regarding those who hold that time is neither conventional nor substantial—namely, Nāgārjuna, Bhāviveka, and others—it is neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because they refute the attachment of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) to time. Furthermore, there are [distinctions of] good and evil, as follows:
The second verse says: "I was originally attached to false views and served as a teacher to various brahmins. At the very time I was so attached, the World-Honored One knew my mind;
he uprooted my errors and spoke of nirvāṇa. When I completely eliminated my false views and returned to the correct path, I attained realization of the Dharma of emptiness.
At the moment I realized this principle, my mind thought to itself: 'I have reached extinction. Thus did I awaken to the truth."
At that time, one now realizes for oneself that this is not true extinction (parinirvāṇa). One immediately awakens to the Great Time (*mahākāla*).

This "time" refers to the state of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) when they are removed; how could it be mundane time? The time of practicing evil is called "evil time," and the time of practicing good is called "good time.

It is within these five aggregates that such times exist. Regarding the seventh [point], the "time of holding and maintaining the precepts": *Note: The text contains several lacunae indicated by □, which have been left as such in the translation.*

This means to exclude their continuity, moments, and so forth. Regarding "retaining" (dhāraṇa), according to the Commentary: it refers to the listener’s faculties being matured such that they evoke the Buddha to preach for them, and so on.
Regarding the eighth point, "general and specific": the general refers simply to the word "at one time. The specific is as explained in the Commentary:
when discussing many dharmas, not specifying a fixed time is called "specific time" (bhinna-kāla).
The Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'not fixed according to the four seasons,' this refers to the refutation of the four-season system.

It would only apply to the capital and the eastern regions; however, from the south of the Ling Mountains northward, the cold and heat differ. How much more so is this the case for the four continents, where such distinctions are natural?
Nevertheless, according to Western custom, the twelve months are divided into three seasons; as stated in the Vinaya, this refers to the final month of spring."
One should seek out a rain-bathing robe during the rainy season, from the sixteenth day of the third month until the fifteenth day of the fourth month;
this constitutes one month. This period continues until the fifteenth day of the seventh month and is called the *varṣā* (rainy) season.

From the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is the cold season (*śīta*). From the fifteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the third month [is the hot season].
"Day" is named *cūḍānta*, which differs from this region [of Jambudvīpa]. "Time" (*kāla*) is called *kalpa* in Sanskrit, which here means "time-division. The Commentary states:

"Because the illumination of the two continents [Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī] arises simultaneously with their functions; for example, when it is noon in the West, it is midnight in the North and the sun has already set in the East.
When it is the time of [the morning watch], it is midday in the West, sunrise in the North, and [midnight] in the East."

It was at midnight; therefore, it is said that he constantly illuminates two continents. Another interpretation is that "time" refers to the four phases (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), namely birth, subsistence, and so forth.
As for the external four phases, these refer to the eons of formation (*vivarta-kalpa*) and subsistence (*sthiti-kalpa*).

There are also the four phases of a single lifetime (*eka-janman*), from birth to old age, and from [youth] to death. Furthermore, in the West (India), there are three seasons, [whereas in the East] there are none.
Regarding the seasons: four months constitute one season. However, the minds of ordinary people are coarse;
they merely perceive the changes of spring, autumn, winter, and summer, yet fail to realize that there are the four great marks (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*) and the four minor marks (*kṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the minor marks, there are nine hundred births and cessations within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). In the space of a finger-snap, there are sixty moments. How [could they perceive this]?
Because one comes to know that a single *kṣaṇa* contains nine hundred births and cessations, it is like tearing silk:
although it is done with a single sound, there is no impediment to the successive severing of the threads. It is also like cutting meat. Thus, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* provides this analogy:

"Ordinary beings perceive only the four great marks (*mahā-lakṣaṇa*), but do not perceive the four minor marks (*kṣudra-lakṣaṇa*). The marks of birth and cessation in each *kṣaṇa* are like fine hairs or motes of dust."
Within the eye, it is extremely obstructive; yet if it were in the hand, there would be no obstruction at all. Ordinary beings are likewise:
because their minds are coarse, they do not perceive the four marks of momentary arising and ceasing. The Noble Ones perceive them, just as a hair in the eye [is perceived].

The Commentary states: "As for the claim that [the term 'one time'] refers to the fact that the four seasons do not circulate universally—though these four seasons are observed in this country, they do not exist in other regions, and it is a universal principle that they are not present everywhere—since this sutra has been circulated in all directions, its specific temporal division cannot be fixed;
therefore, it says 'one time,' which is what people in the world mean by 'at one time' (i.e., at a certain moment). Furthermore, excluding..."
"Below this and so forth" means that, excluding the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, there are the sun and moon below; in the higher realms, the sun and moon cannot move.
Regarding the "nine questions and difficulties," these refer to the subsequent passage concerning those who speak of continuity found within various sūtras.

The meaning here is: since it has already been stated that neither the establishment of time-periods nor the time-periods for preaching the Dharma after attaining enlightenment are permitted, why [is this said]?
For this reason, all sutras speak of "a time" (*ekasmin samaye*). It may also be said that if one speaks of "a time," it encompasses both long and short durations;
indeed, there is not a single one of the twelve periods of the day that is not included therein. How could one bring the specific timing of a separate assembly to bear upon this?
Because the meaning of definitively specifying the time would not be fully comprehensive, they simply say "at one time. Regarding the ten questions and answers: below is the question.
The answer is that the text refers to being "intermediate" regarding purity and impurity. Because these are objective phenomena (*dharma*), it is necessary to definitively specify the location.
As for the time, because it is a transformation of consciousness, no specific time is stated here. Question:
If various durations of time are collectively termed "one time," then since the location is intermediate, should there not be only one location? Answer: Location pertains to the external world.

Regarding the characteristics: as for place, because purity and impurity can be definitively established, and because ordinary beings and sages [intermingle] within time, time is not definitively explained.
Question: Place refers to external characteristics; since purity and impurity differ, place is definitively explained. Time refers to... [omitted];

since ordinary beings and sages differ, time should be definitively explained. Answer: Place refers to phenomena as objective entities (*vastu*). Because external phenomena are coarse, two types of places are explained. As for time... [omitted].
